Heritage & Lineage Born in March 2021 to the Kigelia Female and the White Dam Male. Territory Currently establishing herself in an unconventional area for leopards: Southwestern grasslands Area from Vertical Dam to Cheetah Pools third clearing Open territory largely unoccupied by other female leopards Well-populated with prey species despite open terrain Physical Characteristics 2:2 spot pattern Distinctive orange eyes Pink nose Reproductive History Not yet reproduced – still establishing territory Current Status Newly independent female pioneering territory in the southwestern grasslands, an area traditionally considered unusual for leopards but offering abundant hunting opportunities due to high prey density and limited competition from other females. Behavioural Notes She shows varying levels of comfort with vehicles, occasionally displaying shy behaviour by seeking cover, likely due to less frequent vehicle exposure in her chosen territory. Her comfort in such exposed areas suggests the potential for unique hunting strategies to develop. Historical Significance This represents an interesting case study of leopard adaptability, choosing to establish territory in an area traditionally considered marginal for leopards. Her success could potentially open up a new understanding of leopard habitat utilization at Londolozi. Her presence in the southwestern grasslands helps maintain predator balance in an area historically less frequented by leopards.

leopards.excerpt: Twin daughter of the Ntsumi Female and Nweti Male, born August 2023. Now navigating independence along Londolozi's southern boundary.
leopards.profile: The Kurhula 3:3 Female arrived as part of a twin litter, born around August 2023 to the Ntsumi 3:3 Female and sired by the Nweti Male, a dominant and exceptionally relaxed male who held a vast territory across the southeastern reaches of Londolozi for the better part of a decade. She and her twin sister, the Mgiba 3:3 Female, are among the Nweti Male’s most recent offspring, and with him believed to have passed in early 2025, they now represent one of the clearest threads of his legacy on this land. The Kurhula 3:3 Female has been seen periodically along the eastern portion of Londolozi’s southern boundary as she navigates the early stages of independence. Where her sister has moved further south toward the Sabi River, Kurhula has remained closer to the ground she was raised on — beginning the process of establishing herself in a landscape that, for a young female, is both familiar and fiercely contested. She is still finding her feet. That, in itself, is worth watching.

leopards.title: Mother Leopard 2:2 Female
leopards.name: Mother Leopard
leopards.excerpt: The original viewable leopard of Londolozi, if not Africa. In 1979 this leopard appeared as if by magic, allowing vehicles to view her.
leopards.profile: She did not announce herself. She simply stayed. In 1979, on a morning that looked like every other morning in the Sabi Sand, a young female leopard was found in the drainage lines south of the Londolozi camps. She was watchful and uncertain — but she did not run. That single choice, made by a wild animal on no particular morning, changed the course of Londolozi’s history more completely than anything that came before or after it. John Varty and tracker Elmon Mhlongo spent the next twelve years of their lives following her. They adjusted their hours to match hers, sleeping through the heat of the day to be with her at night. They documented her hunts, her cubs, her territorial movements. In doing so, they captured moments no camera had ever been permitted to see, including the first filmed mating sequence of wild leopards ever recorded. That footage became Silent Hunter , the documentary that brought Londolozi to the attention of the world. She had a 2:2 spot pattern and a temperament that became legendary. Over the course of her life, she raised nine litters, from which twelve cubs reached independence, a breeding record that remains unmatched at Londolozi. Through her daughters and their daughters, she founded a dynasty that now reaches eight generations. Her descendants include the 3:4 Female, the Dudley Riverbank Female, and the Ndzanzeni Female. She died in 1991 at approximately sixteen years of age. The exact circumstances were never determined. She had, by then, done something that no one had believed possible: she had demonstrated that trust between a wild leopard and a human being was not only possible, but repeatable. Her cubs were habituated to vehicles. Their cubs were habituated. And so it continued, generation by generation, until the leopard-viewing that Londolozi is known for today became simply the way things were. There is nothing at Londolozi that marks where she walked or what she left behind. There doesn’t need to be. Her legacy is not something you can point to, it is something you feel the moment a leopard holds your gaze from a branch above the road and does not look away. That feeling, repeated across five decades and thousands of people, is what she began. Every morning that a tracker follows fresh prints in the sand of the Maxabene, it continues. Every afternoon that a leopard holds a visitor’s gaze without looking away, it continues still.
leopards.territory: The Mother Leopard held territory around central Sparta for the duration of her life. The Maxabene drainage line, where this female was first seen, lay at the heart of the territory and provided her with ideal hunting opportunities on its heavily vegetated banks, whilst the tangled root systems provided den sites in which to raise her cubs. Today this still area remains as heavily contested territory for both male and female leopards.

leopards.excerpt: Born 1984, fierce daughter of Mother Leopard. Her unpredictable nature challenged rangers, legacy lived on through 3:4 Female.
leopards.profile: Named after the Tugwaan Drainage central in her territory Heritage & Lineage Born in April 1984 to the original Mother Leopard, representing an intriguing contrast to her mother’s relaxed nature. Despite her aggressive temperament, she proved to be a crucial link in Londolozi’s most prestigious leopard lineage through her daughter, the 3:4 Female. Territory Established territory in and around the Tugwaan riverbed shortly after reaching independence at about one year of age. Her territory would later be inherited by her daughter, the 3:4 Female, maintaining the family’s presence in this significant area. Physical Characteristics 2:3 spot pattern Notably aggressive posture around vehicles Commanding presence that demanded respect Reproductive History Most notable offspring: 1992: Gave birth to the legendary 3:4 Female Known as an excellent mother despite her fierce nature High success rate in raising cubs Behavioural Notes Famous for her unpredictable and often aggressive nature: Completely relaxed at night but notoriously aggressive during the day Would charge vehicles and people on foot without warning Required special vehicle positioning techniques for safe viewing Never fully habituated despite 16 years of viewing Demonstrated remarkable contrast between daytime and nighttime behaviour Required elaborate safety protocols for tracking on foot Historical Significance The Tugwaan Female represents a fascinating chapter in Londolozi’s leopard history: Proved that even direct descendants of habituated leopards can maintain wild tendencies Demonstrated the individual nature of leopard personalities Successfully raised the 3:4 Female who would become one of Londolozi’s most photographed leopards Became legendary among rangers and trackers for her unpredictable nature Her reputation lives on in ranger stories and analogies Served as a constant reminder of leopards’ true wild nature despite habituation Her legacy extends beyond her fearsome reputation through her daughter, the 3:4 Female, who showed that an aggressive mother could produce a remarkably relaxed offspring, challenging assumptions about inherited behaviour in leopards.

leopards.excerpt: Born to the Tugwaan female in August 1992, this leopard would redefine the relationship between man and wild cat.
leopards.profile: Named after 3:4 spot pattern but, known affectionately as “Manana” (Mother in Shangaan) by John Varty Heritage & Lineage Born in August 1992 to the notoriously aggressive Tugwaan Female and granddaughter of the original Mother Leopard. Her remarkable contrast to her mother’s temperament demonstrated the individual nature of leopard personalities while maintaining the prestigious bloodline’s significance at Londolozi. Territory Established territory in and around the Tugwaan Drainage and surrounds, particularly favouring Nyamakunze Crest. After her death, this prime territory was inherited by her daughter, the Nottens Female, maintaining the family’s presence in this significant area. Physical Characteristics 3:4 spot pattern Notably relaxed demeanor around vehicles Athletic build characteristic of the Mother Leopard lineage Reproductive History Demonstrated remarkable reproductive success: Attempted to raise 8 litters by age 11 Notable successful offspring include: Nottens Female (first litter) – lived to 18 years, Londolozi’s longest-lived recorded leopard Dudley Riverbank Female (September 1998 litter) Uniquely adopted and raised her grandson (Dudley Riverbank 5:5 Male) after her daughter abandoned him during a hyena attack Current Status Passed away in the winter of 2009 at almost 17 years of age. Her death drew visitors from far and wide to pay respects, marking the end of an era but not the end of her legacy, which continues through her descendants. Behavioural Notes Revolutionized understanding of leopard behaviour in several ways: Showed extraordinary comfort around vehicles despite her mother’s aggressive nature Demonstrated unprecedented maternal behaviour by adopting her grandson Formed a unique bond with her adopted grandson who later provided for her in her old age Developed a special trust relationship with John Varty Known for remarkable hunting abilities, including documented python kills Historical Significance The 3:4 Female represents a pivotal figure in Londolozi’s leopard history: Bridged the gap between her aggressive mother and the relaxed nature of future generations Challenged conventional understanding of leopard behaviour through her adoption of her grandson Established a significant portion of the current Mother Leopard lineage through her successful daughters Her death in 2009 marked the end of an era, but her legacy continues through her descendants Demonstrated the individual nature of leopard personalities, showing how offspring can differ dramatically from their parents Her story remains one of the most compelling in Londolozi’s leopard history, particularly her unprecedented relationship with her grandson, which challenged the scientific understanding of leopard behaviour.

Physical Characteristics 5:5 spot pattern Large pale body typical of Mother Leopard descendants Dark alluring eyes Distinctive ageing features in later years Reproductive History Despite multiple attempts throughout her life: 1998: First and most successful litter – two females reached independence (including Piva Female) 2001: Two cubs (both lost) 2002: Two cubs (both lost) 2003: Two cubs (fate uncertain) 2005: Two cubs (one taken by Martial Eagle) 2008: Two cubs (both lost) Multiple mating attempts in later years (2009-2012) proved unsuccessful Behavioural Notes Demonstrated remarkable adaptability in her later years, shifting territories as she aged and felt pressure from younger females. leopards.excerpt: This leopard was the first cub of the Nottens female, and therefore inherited the royal blood of the original Mother Leopard.
leopards.profile: This leopard was the first cub of the Nottens female, and therefore inherited the royal blood of the original Mother Leopard. She established territory in the far south east of Londolozi, getting her name from Piva Pan, a small waterhole where she spent much of her time when first independent. She wasn’t viewed often on Londolozi, spending the majority of her time beyond our southern boundary, but would occasionally venture back north, especially when raising litters as the area around Piva Pan itself offers numerous densites in the form of rocky clusters. One of her notable litters, born in early 2010, included a young male who grew up to become the Piva male, dominant over the south eastern regions of Londolozi. His sister was killed around the age of 8 months by the Tugwaan male but the male survived to independence. In early 2016 the Piva female was seen in very poor condition near Kirkman’s Camp in the southern reaches of the Sabi Sands. It is suspected that in her old age (over 17 years) she was pushed out of her territory by a younger, stronger leopard (possibly Hlarulini female from the south) and was forced into a nomadic lifestyle.
leopards.territory: Although rarely seen on Londolozi, this leopard's territory fell into eastern Sparta and eastern Dudley. She raised a few litters around a waterhole called Piva Pan from which she got her name. This area has dense drainage lines and rocky bands making it fairly inaccessible and ideal for hiding small cubs.

leopards.title: Dudley Riverbank 5:5 Male
leopards.name: Dudley Riverbank
leopards.death_note: Mauled by Tsalala pride in Manyelethi River. Died of his wounds.
leopards.excerpt: Incredibly, the 5:5 male was adopted as a cub by his grandmother, the 3:4 female, and raised by her to adulthood.
leopards.profile: The story of this leopard has become the stuff of legend. Feeding off a kill with his mother as a cub, the 5:5 young male was somehow adopted by the 3:4 female after she brought her cub to feed on the same kill. Unbelievably, this old leopard took it upon herself to raise this cub of her daughter, and it was solely thanks to her efforts that he survived to independence. A further twist in the tale was that when the 3:4 female was old and becoming infirm, the 5:5 male was seen sharing kills with her on multiple occasions. Male leopards are not known for sharing kills with females, but the fact that this male repeatedly did so with the 3:4 female suggests some very strong tie not previously documented in leopards in the wild. Upon approaching full size, the 5:5 male began encroaching into the Camp Pan male’s territory around the Londolozi camps, and for a while looked set to establish himself and topple the older male, but the disappearance of the Emsagwen 4:6 male in the east left a territory vacant, and the 5:5 male simply headed there instead. He has remained there to this day, despite losing the use of his left eye, possibly in a fight with another leopard. As of mid 2015 the 5:5 male has started being seen in a number of spots far outside his usual territory, suggesting that he is under pressure from other another male(s) or has already been ousted. He is believed to have killed the October 2015 litter of the Tamboti female.
leopards.territory: A male that claimed territory fairly easily in eastern Marthly upon the disappearance of the Emsagwen male. We continue to see this male occasionally around the eastern portion of Londolozi, both north and south of the Sand River.

leopards.profile: Directly descended from the original mother leopard and therefore part of the royal lineage of Londolozi, the Piva male was born to the Piva female beyond our southern borders. Born in 2010 in a litter of two, his sibling was killed by the Tugwaan male leopard later that year, but the Piva male survived to independence, moving into the southern reaches of Londolozi during his nomadic years and occasionally being seen during 2012 and 2013. In 2014 he began establishing himself properly in the south east, forcing out the old Camp Pan male and taking over a territory that runs from the north eastern corner of Londolozi almost to the Tugwaan riverbed in the south. He is easily recognized by the distinctive oval of spots on his forehead.

leopards.excerpt: Royal descendant of Mother Leopard lineage. Remarkable single cub success story who overcame injury to continue the royal bloodline.
leopards.profile: Heritage & Lineage Born in March 2012 to the Dudley Riverbank Female and sired by the Tugwaan Male, the Ndzanzeni Female holds a particularly special place in Londolozi’s leopard dynasty. As the great, great-granddaughter of the original Mother Leopard, she represents one of the few remaining direct descendants of this historic lineage. Her birth as a single cub was actually advantageous – her mother, at almost 14 years old, could focus all her energy on raising this sole offspring, typical of older leopards who rarely successfully raise more than one cub at that age. Territory Following in her mother’s footsteps, she initially established herself in the territory that the Dudley Riverbank Female once controlled in the deep south and east of Londolozi. Her current range stretches from the Sand River all the way across to the western grasslands. She has shown remarkable stability in maintaining this territory, remaining in roughly the same area since reaching independence. Physical Characteristics Distinctive 4:3 spot pattern Historically recognizable by her noticeable limp on the back left leg Reproductive History The Ndzanzeni Female has demonstrated remarkable persistence in her reproductive efforts: Successful Offspring: Tortoise Pan Male (August 2016) – Her greatest success story and currently the only offspring raised to independence Notable Attempts: December 2015: Two cubs (only seen once at around 2 months before loss) August 2016: Two cubs at Python Rocks (female cub lost, male survived – Tortoise Pan Male) Mid 2020: Two cubs (litter lost at about 8 months) Late 2021: Two cubs (male and female, lost at nine months old) May 2022: Suspected den site (cubs never viewed) March 2023: Suckle marks observed (den not located) September 2023: Two cubs in Umkumbe (litter lost) May 2024: Denned in Sand River then Piva drainage (litter lost) November 2024: Suspected den site (cubs never viewed) Current Status Continues to maintain her territory successfully in the southern regions of Dudley. Her recovery from a severe leg injury that nearly prevented her from walking demonstrates her exceptional resilience. Despite several setbacks with recent litter, she continues to contribute to the population dynamics of the area. Behavioural Notes Perhaps her most remarkable achievement was successfully raising the Tortoise Pan Male while suffering from a debilitating injury to her back left leg. During this period, she could barely put weight on the leg, yet managed to hunt and provide for her cub. This display of determination and adaptability speaks to the incredible resilience of these cats. Historical Significance The Ndzanzeni Female’s story is one of remarkable success against the odds. Born as a single cub to an ageing mother, discovered by skilled tracker Freddy Ngobeni at Paul’s Crossing, and going on to successfully raise her own cub despite severe injury, she embodies the resilience of Londolozi’s leopards. As one of the few remaining direct descendants of the Mother Leopard lineage, she represents a crucial link to Londolozi’s leopard history, maintaining the legacy through her son, the Tortoise Pan Male.
leopards.territory: A leopard who holds territory in south-east Dudley, essentially having adopted her late mother's territory. Whilst trying to raise her first litter she spent the vast majority of her time in the Tugwaan drainage, close to where her mother denned her and thus an area she is very familiar with.

leopards.excerpt: Initially calm and graceful, this resilient female overcame partial blindness to continue hunting and raising cubs in western Londolozi.
leopards.profile: Heritage & Lineage First encountered in 1991 as an adult leopard, the origins of the Mhangeni Female remain unknown. Though her early lineage is unclear, she established an important bloodline through her daughter, the Maxabene Female, and her son, the Mhangeni Male. Territory Originally established in western Londolozi Gradually pushed further west by her daughter, the Maxabene Female Maintained territory in western Sparta extending into Castleton Notable for defending territory despite visual impairment Physical Characteristics 2:3 spot pattern Most recognizable feature was her milky right eye (from 2002 cobra encounter) Distinctive disability made her easily identifiable Known for calm demeanour around vehicles Reproductive History Demonstrated persistence in reproduction despite numerous setbacks: Successful Offspring: January 1998: Maxabene Female (female cub reached independence despite early abandonment) June 2000: Mhangeni Male (reached independence at 2 years) Other Attempts: June 1996: Two cubs (killed by spotted hyenas) January 1997: Two cubs (killed by lions) January 1998: Male cub killed by lions June 2000: Female cub died at 6 months Behavioural Notes Remarkably calm nature around vehicles despite challenges Adapted hunting techniques after losing sight in one eye, demonstrated remarkable resilience after cobra encounter. Known for rarely hoisting kills, which may have contributed to cub losses Maintained territorial behaviour despite visual impairment Sometimes abandoned cubs earlier than typical. Historical Significance Proved leopards could adapt to significant physical challenges Contributed to Londolozi’s leopard population through two successful offspring Demonstrated the challenges of raising cubs in a predator-rich environment Her story highlights the constant threats faced by leopards Through the Maxabene Female, her bloodline continued in the area Her story serves as a testament to the resilience of leopards, showing how they can adapt to severe injuries while continuing to hunt and raise cubs in challenging conditions. Her legacy lives on through her daughter, the Maxabene Female, who went on to establish herself in prime territory.
leopards.territory: This female held territory around western Sparta and into Castleton. These areas are predominantly open grassland and thus lack a huge amount of cover. This serves as a good example of how adaptable these cats are, as the Mhangeni female was very successful huntress. There are a number of Marula trees in this area that would have helped as vantage and hoisting points.

leopards.territory: With a long, thin territory this female was eventually named after the land she claimed along the Maxabene Riverbed in central Sparta. Guests still speak to this day of the magnificent viewing she provided with her youngsters in this drainage line; playing and hunting amongst its tall, well-established trees.

leopards.title: Mhangeni 2:2 Male
leopards.name: Mhangeni
leopards.excerpt: Born in June of 2000 to the Mhangeni female, the Mhangeni male moved south to eventually to establish his territory.
leopards.profile: Born in June of 2000 to the Mhangeni female, the Mhangeni male moved south to eventually establish territory in the far southern reaches of Londolozi, with the bulk of his territory lying beyond our borders. Known in the south as the Sand River male, he sired a number of cubs with females in that area, with one of them, the Piva male, eventually moving back into Londolozi to establish territory in 2014. In later life he lost the use of his right eye to unknown causes; some speculate it was in a territorial fight, others suggest a spitting cobra, which in itself would be a cruel twist of irony as this was exactly what happened to his mother. He became nomadic again in late 2013 and the last recorded sightings of him are from the winter of 2014.
leopards.territory: A leopard that held territory in southern Dudley, but mainly further south of that; prime habitat for the movement of medium sized antelope, consistent water sources as well as a high density of females.

leopards.title: Makhotini 3:3 Male
leopards.name: Makhotini
leopards.death_note: Unsure of when
leopards.excerpt: The brother of the Tu-Tones male from the same litter, the Makhotini male has had a far more successful life.
leopards.profile: The brother of the Tu-Tones male from the same litter, the Makhotini male has had a far more successful life. Dispersing at around three years of age, as is normal for young male leopards, he moved into the south western grasslands of Londolozi, an area not renowned for its leopard population, but by virtue of that fact, not hotly competed for. Slowly this leopard expanded his territory further to the south and west, eventually venturing far beyond Londolozi’s borders to control a substantial portion of Sabi Sabi, as well as the far south-eastern corner of Singita. He has mated with a number of females in the area and sired cubs with the Little Bush female. It is likely that he fathered the Tatowa female’s first litter as well. General game numbers differ in much of his territory, and the Makhotini male has adapted by hunting a larger variety of prey than other leopards. He has been seen hunting buffalo calves out of large herds on a number of occasions, and reedbuck and aardvark are some of the more unusual prey species that he has been recorded catching.
leopards.territory: This leopard has established a large territory which extends from south west Dudley over much of Sabi Sabi. One of the reasons his territory is so large is that the open grasslands which dominate the area are not as flush with general game, and therefore not as desirable as hunting habitat. Fewer females inhabit the area and so the Makhotini male is forced to roam far to access mating opportunities.

leopards.title: Tu-Tones 3:2 Male
leopards.name: Tu-Tones
leopards.death_note: Unknown
leopards.excerpt: The Tu Tones male astounded everyone by establishing his territory within his father Camp Pan's territory.
leopards.profile: Originally the Maxabene 3:2 young male, and born in the same litter as the Makhotini male, the Tu-Tones male was an individual that single-handedly rewrote the textbooks on leopard behaviour. His movements upon independence were probably a result of a combination of factors, but essentially what happened was that he didn’t disperse as young males generally do, but instead stayed pretty much within the confines of his father’s territory. Another behavioural anomaly was that his father (the Camp Pan male) seemed to accept his presence; although there was some snarling and aggression towards each other when they met, there was no physical confrontation witnessed. The death of his mother and the fact that the one female cub she raised to independence had dispersed a long way away meant that there was no real genetic pressure for him to disperse either. Whatever the case, the Tu-Tones male was an almost constant presence in the territory controlled by the Camp Pan male, and the two were even seen sharing mating rights with the Tamboti female on at least two separate occasions. Unfortunately for this young male, his unusual co-territorial occupation with his father was to be his downfall, as once the Camp Pan male became unseated in 2014 by the Piva male, the Tu-Tones male, having not been properly territorial himself, seems to have been unable to maintain any kind of hold on the territory his father had been defending, and was forced into a nomadic lifestyle almost overnight. His condition deteriorated very quickly from there, and he was last seen on Londolozi in the late Summer of 2015. He was found dead to the east of our boundary in late March of that year, and tracks in the area suggested that a troop of baboons had killed him. His emaciated condition would have made him incredibly vulnerable.
leopards.territory: A remarkable story in which this leopard established his territory in eastern Sparta within the territory of his father (something that is typical of female but not male leopards). He died prematurely at the age of 7, close to the time of death of his father and thus we were not able to see how the extension of his territory would have played out.

leopards.title: Nyelethi 4:4 Female
leopards.name: Nyelethi
leopards.excerpt: Powerful descendant of Saseka Female, a skilled huntress defied odds by raising intact litter of three cubs to independence in Londolozi.
leopards.profile: Heritage & Lineage Born in 2003 to the Saseka Female Carried forward the impressive hunting abilities of her bloodline Notable for her notched left ear Established a significant presence in northern territories Territory Initially inhabited her mother’s territory north of Londolozi boundary Established control over western and southern portions of mother’s range in 2008 Core territory centered around western bank of Manyelethi River Known for utilizing dense riverine vegetation Territory particularly rich in prey species Physical Characteristics 4:4 spot pattern Notched left ear Large, powerful build Reproductive History Successful Offspring: March 2008: Two females (one killed by Newington Male, Mbilo Female killed by Majingilane males in 2010) July 2009: Three cubs (rare intact litter of three reached independence): Nanga Female (3:3) Nyelethi Male (4:3) Nyelethi Young Male (3:2) Behavioural Notes Exceptional hunter known for devastating efficiency Remarkable mother who successfully raised three cubs simultaneously Utilized dense riverine vegetation for denning and hunting Demonstrated excellent maternal care, particularly evident in raising triple litter Historical Significance Successfully raised one of the few recorded intact litters of three cubs Demonstrated exceptional maternal abilities despite challenging conditions Her territory selection and hunting prowess enabled the successful raising of multiple cubs The legacy continues through descendants, particularly through the Nanga Female Provided valuable insights into maternal behaviour through extensive documentation Her successful triple litter challenged the conventional understanding of leopard cub survival rates Her disappearance in 2011 marked the end of an era in northern Londolozi, but her legacy lives on through her offspring, particularly her daughter the Nanga Female who went on to establish territory in similar areas.
leopards.territory: In her later years, this female established her territory around western and central Marthly, focusing her time around the Manyelethi River. With pools of water, dense vegetation, rocky sections, overhanging roots, a plethora of visiting game and a soft sand in which to hunt silently, many leopards have made this part of Londolozi their home and will continue to do so in the future.

leopards.profile: This leopard was born to the Nyelethi female in March 2008, but sadly did not live long enough to establish herself among the more prominent Londolozi leopards. Upon independence she spent much time in the east of her mother’s territory, around Nanga road and further east towards the Maliliwane drainage line, but she was killed by one of the Majingilane male lions to the north of the Londolozi boundary in September 2010.
leopards.territory: At the time of her death this leopard was just becoming territorial around north-eastern Marthly. This territory is now held by the Nanga and Malilwane females and varies from riverine bush to mixed woodland and combretum dominated thickets. A prevalence of water in the area means there is a decent variety of game to be found here year round.

leopards.territory: This leopard's territory falls into north and central Marthly. Prominent water holes like Nanga Pan and Mahlahla Dam as well as the seasonal Manyelethi River help to sustain this leopard year round. A band of rocky outcrops which fall into her territory and form the section where her and the Tutlwa female's territory meet, are also prime den sites and have been used by this leopard for her last few litters.

leopards.title: Nyelethi 2:3 Young Male
leopards.name: Nyelethi
leopards.excerpt: He was born in 2009 in a litter of three, with his siblings being the Nanga female and Nyelethi 4:3 male.
leopards.profile: Little is known of the fate of this male. He was born in 2009 in a litter of three, with his siblings being the Nanga female and Nyelethi 4:3 male, who established territory in the western sector of the Sabi Sands. It is very unusual for a litter of three to all survive to independence. The last records of him are on Londolozi soil, and he was last seen in the early parts of 2012. As a young independent male, he would have had to survive at least a few years before being old and big enough to establish a territory of his own. Whether he managed to do this or not remains a mystery. No records of him after 2012 exist, but it is certainly possible that he displaced to the Kruger National Park. Since leopards – males in particular – regularly displace into the Sabi Sands from KNP, they can easily displace the other way. He may have been killed by a rival predator, but we hope he made it into the Kruger and established a reign as successful as his brother.
leopards.territory: Status of this leopard's territory is unknown.

leopards.title: Nyelethi 4:3 Male
leopards.name: Nyelethi
leopards.excerpt: Born to the Nyelethi female in 2009, this male was one of three cubs that all survived to independence.
leopards.profile: Born to the Nyelethi female in 2009, this male was one of three cubs that all survived to independence. His sister is the Nanga female and his brother the Nyelethi 2:3 male, who dispersed northwards, while the 4:3 brother moved south and west. Initially spending time around the Londolozi camps, tolerated to a degree by the Marthly male (believed to be his father), he eventually dispersed westwards, establishing territory in Singita and Othawa. This male rose in notoriety when he killed the Ravenscourt female in June 2013 when she was trying to protect her cub (now the Ravenscourt male, seen in southern Singita). He has established himself in the western sections of Singita and Othawa, but does have quite a significant territorial overlap with the Kaxane male in the southern reaches of the Singita property.
leopards.territory: Since independence this male has established himself in western Singita and Castleton.

leopards.profile: Named after the Makomsava road where she was frequently seen in her early independence Heritage & Lineage Born in September 2016 to the Nanga Female and sired by the Anderson Male, she represents the continuing legacy of the Saseka Female lineage. Born in a litter of two, though her sibling disappeared at approximately five months of age. Territory Initially established in her mother’s former territory along the Manyelethi River system, particularly around the Leadwood forest. Her territory has shifted significantly over time, expanding westward towards Ximpalapala koppie in late 2019. Currently, she maintains a territory primarily north of Londolozi’s boundary, though recently showing increasing presence back on the reserve. Physical Characteristics 2:2 spot pattern Facial features characteristic of the Saseka lineage Reproductive History Has faced significant challenges in her reproductive efforts: Attempts: Mid 2020: Two cubs denned at Marthly Pools (litter lost) October 2021: Two cubs north of boundary (Young Female reached independence) June 2022: Two cubs born north of the boundary (litter lost) November 2024: Currently believed to be denning with two cubs north of the boundary Current Status Currently raising what’s believed to be a litter of two cubs, denned north of Londolozi’s boundary. Shows increasing presence back on Londolozi property, suggesting possible territory expansion or shift. Behavioural Notes Demonstrated remarkable adaptability in her territorial movements, particularly in response to pressure from other females. Her early establishment in the Leadwood forest area showed excellent strategic thinking in terms of hunting territory. The loss of several litters hasn’t diminished her reproductive efforts, showing the persistence characteristic of successful female leopards. Historical Significance Represents an interesting case study in territorial flexibility among Londolozi’s leopards. Her mother’s complete ceding of territory to her was unusual, and her subsequent movements northward and recent returns to Londolozi demonstrate the dynamic nature of leopard territories. While facing challenges in raising cubs to independence, her recent success with one female offspring suggests growing maturity and experience as a mother.
leopards.territory: This leopard is usually viewed in central Marthly (the section of Londolozi north of the Sand River). Late 2019 saw her pushing territory west into the area previously held by the Ingrid Dam female.

leopards.excerpt: This female was a small leopard with a shorter than average tail. She was territorial around the western reaches of Londolozi ’s Sand River.
leopards.profile: This female was a small leopard with a shorter than average tail. She was territorial around the western reaches of Londolozi ’s Sand River frontage, but as most of her territory lay north of the river, sightings of her only became consistent after the purchase of the Marthly property in 1999. She raised a number of cubs to independence, the most notable of which are the Ximpalapala female, who although skittish is still seen in her mother’s old territory, and the Tugwaan male, who dispersed into the south east. These two were born in the same litter in 2001 The last sighting of the short tailed female was in 2003, when she was seen in poor condition with a missing ear and cuts all over her. She was not seen after that and it is presumed that she died of her wounds.
leopards.territory: Deep gully systems, a small portion of the Sand River, portions of open clearing and thick mixed woodland provided this female with a diverse and optimal territory in western Marthly.

leopards.title: Tugwaan 5:4 Male
leopards.name: Tugwaan
leopards.death_note: Carcass discovered on Mala Mala. Bite marks on back, possibly killed by lions.
leopards.excerpt: A beautiful male with a distinctive “V” shape on his forehead, the Tugwaan male was dominant for many years over a huge territory.
leopards.profile: A beautiful male with a distinctive “V” shape on his forehead, the Tugwaan male was dominant for many years over a huge territory that stretched from beyond the Sand River in the east almost to the western boundary of the Sabi Sand. Born to the Short-tailed female in Marthly in 2001 in the same litter as the Ximpalapala female, he began moving south and east, establishing himself during the latter part of 2004 in the eastern sections of Londolozi. From there his territorial shift was southwards, possibly due to pressure from the bigger Camp Pan male. The Tugwaan male in his prime held territory centred along the Tugwaan riverbed, which is where he got his name, but he was encountered as north of the Maxabene and even beyond Londolozi’s southern borders. In later life he suffered from the knock-on effect of an influx of males from the north. The Marthly male pushed south, which in turn forced the Camp Pan male south, which led the the Tugwaan male being displaced to the south and east of Londolozi and rarely seen. At the time of writing the Tugwaan male is 15 years old and in the twilight of his life. Although it is difficult to assign paternity to cubs, as females will mate with multiple males, it is almost certain that the Tugwaan male sired the Ndzanzeni female, and has done his part to incorporate his genes in the royal lineage of Londolozi.
leopards.territory: Males typically have a much larger territory than females but the Tugwaan male had a particularly large one that stretched almost the width of the Sabi Sands, incorporating many habitat types. With the movement of other dominant males in his later years, his territory was shifted to south-east Dudley and south of that towards the Sabie River, still prime habitat for leopard.

leopards.profile: Named after the Ximpalapala Koppie in the north due to her spending a lot of time around that area. Heritage & Lineage Born in 2001 to the Short Tailed Female Sister to the Tugwaan Male Bloodline continued through the Tatowa Female Part of a successful northern leopard lineage Territory Initially grew up in neighboring Othawa property Expanded eastward into NW Londolozi after Nyelethi Female’s death (2011) Core territory centred around: Ximpalapala Koppie Northwestern sectors Areas with limited vehicle access The territory was characterized by rocky outcrops and dense vegetation Physical Characteristics 4:4 spot pattern Notably wary demeanor around vehicles Distinctive furtive movement patterns Reproductive History Most notable offspring: Early 2012: Three cubs (litter including Tatowa Female) Two cubs lost to Gowrie Male Tatowa Female successfully reached independence Successfully raised at least one female to continue the lineage Behavioural Notes Remained extremely elusive and skilled at avoiding detection throughout her life Mastered use of challenging terrain to maintain privacy Maintained limited habituation despite years of territory overlap with vehicles Exhibited strategic den site selection in rocky areas Demonstrated excellent maternal abilities despite skittish nature Specialized in utilizing areas with minimal vehicle access Showed slight relaxation around vehicles only in her final years Historical Significance Represented successful adaptation to human presence while maintaining wild nature Demonstrated how unhabituated leopards could thrive alongside the viewed population Successfully raised the Tatowa Female who became more relaxed than her mother Provided valuable insights into leopard behaviour in less-viewed areas Her story highlighted the diversity of leopard personalities at Londolozi Legacy continued through more relaxed offspring Her disappearance in 2016 marked the end of an era in northwestern Londolozi, opening territory for the Ingrid Dam Female and her daughter. Through her daughter the Tatowa Female, her genes continued in the population, though manifesting in a more relaxed individual. Her story served as a reminder that even in an area known for viewable leopards, some individuals maintained their secretive nature while still successfully raising the next generation.
leopards.territory: A leopard named after a rocky outcrop in western Marthly, where she has been encountered in the past. It seems she established a territory to the west of Londolozi and expanded it to include the western section of Marthly upon the death of the Nyelethi female. Due to the inaccessibility of this rocky section, the dense thickets surrounding it and her fairly skittish nature, this is not a leopard we see particularly often but the area does provide her with a multitude of game to hunt, including the rock dwelling Klipspringer.

leopards.title: Tatowa 3:3 Female
leopards.name: Tatowa
leopards.death_note: Unknown
leopards.excerpt: The Tatowa female was one of a litter of three females born in early 2012 to the Ximpalapala female of the north.
leopards.profile: This leopard is a bit of an anomaly, as she was born to a female who remains very skittish around vehicles, yet her cubs grew up far more relaxed than her. The Tatowa female was one of a litter of three females born in early 2012 to the Ximpalapala female of the north. The litter was first confirmed when viewed on top of Ximpalapala koppie, and viewing over the next few months was pretty special, with three young cubs observed almost daily, playing around up on the rocks. As the cubs got to decide their own level of exposure to the vehicles by descending or ascending the koppie as they pleased, it wasn’t long before they were relaxed enough around the Land Rovers to be venturing down to ground level by themselves. Interestingly enough, when their mother returned her influence would turn them skittish again, and viewing tended to be far better when she was not around. Towards the end of 2012 the Gowrie male claimed the territory of Ximpalapala koppie and the surrounding areas, and we believe he killed two of the cubs in the litter, with the 3:3 young female alone surviving. After a few forays into the southern reaches of Londolozi she eventually established territory quite far to the south, and as she was viewed in the vicinity of Tatowa Dam on a number of occasions, was given the name Tatowa female. She was seen heavily pregnant in early 2016 and was believed to be denning somewhere in the deep south of Londolozi, but after she was viewed mating with the Inyathini male with no signs of suckle marks a few weeks later, it was presumed the litter had been lost.
leopards.territory: The Tatowa female's territory falls on south and central Dudley. For a female, particularly a young female, she may have a large territory because a significant portion of it falls in open grassland and as a result it is harder for her to hunt or to find suitable den sites. It may also be that there is less competition for this slightly less suitable leopard habitat.

leopards.profile: The Campbell Koppies female was born to the Sunset Bend female in September 1999 in a litter of three, and was officially independent when her mother birthed another litter of three in October 2001 and became more aggressive towards her. She established territory to the north and east of Londolozi, and had only two surviving offspring; the Ostrich Koppies female who is territorial to the east of our boundary was born in 2004 and the Maliliwane female who died in early 2016 was born in in 2007. Other litters were almost certainly born (one in early 2004 almost) but none of these cubs survived to independence. One would have thought that a leopard with such an abundance of good den sites in her territory (the Campbell Koppies themselves) would have had better success in raising cubs, but it was not to be. The Campbell Koppies female was last seen in mid 2013, and would have been just shy of 14 years old at the time of her death.

leopards.excerpt: Daughter of Sunset Bend Female, this resilient leopard raised at least 5 cubs to independence before a tragic end defending her final litter
leopards.profile: Named after the Shangaan word xidulu for termite mound. Heritage & Lineage Born October 2001 to the Sunset Bend Female Inherited distinctive golden coat of the Sunset Bend lineage Sister to Ravenscourt Female Successfully continued prestigious bloodline through multiple offspring Territory Although her initial territory covered much of eastern Londolozi to our eastern neighbours (where she was called the Kikilezi Female), she subsequently moved steadily north and east and was seldom encountered on Londolozi leading up to her death. The territory included diverse terrain from dense riverine thickets along Sand River to the wide open clearings dotted with numerous termite mounds. Physical Characteristics 2:3 spot pattern Rich golden coat characteristic of Sunset Bend lineage Athletic build maintained into senior years Distinctive ageing features in later life, such as tattered ears and sunken eyes. Reproductive History Demonstrated remarkable success as a mother, raising at least five cubs to independence: 2013: Piccadilly Female and Sibuye Female 2016: Three Rivers Female, a male sibling also survived and dispersed (cubs approximately 11 months old at the time of her death) Behavioural Notes Exceptional mother even in advanced age Known for fierce defence of territory and cubs Skilled at utilizing dense riverine vegetation for denning Notable for aggressive defence of kills against other leopards Successfully navigated complex territorial dynamics with neighbouring females Historical Significance A crucial link in perpetuating the Sunset Bend lineage Successfully raised cubs in areas with the highest predator density Demonstrated exceptional parenting abilities into advanced age The final act of defending cubs at age 16 exemplified maternal dedication Her story highlighted the challenges faced by ageing leopards The legacy continued through multiple surviving offspring Provided valuable insights into leopard maternal behaviour Her death in 2017 at the hands of male lions, possibly while defending her cubs, marked the end of a remarkable life that exemplified the resilience and maternal dedication of Londolozi’s leopards. At almost 16 years old, she had successfully navigated one of the most predator-rich environments to raise multiple generations of cubs, contributing significantly to the continuation of the prestigious Sunset Bend lineage.

leopards.profile: A young female who was not often seen during her time on Londolozi, owing to her inhabiting a not-often traversed section of the property. The far north-east has few roads, and sightings of this female were few and far between. She was easily recognised by her pink nose and the distinct notch in her left ear. She was born in 2007 to the Campbell Koppies female, herself a daughter of the legendary Sunset Bend female. A few of her recorded 5 litters have been viewed briefly, but so far only one cub seems to have survived; a female from the 2014 litter. A further litter was viewed briefly during winter of 2015 but disappeared shortly afterwards. After not having been seen for a few months, reports from the reserves north of Londolozi indicated that this female was raising a litter of three at the beginning of 2016. Sadly however, her condition was also reported as very poor, and it was theorised that she may have been bitten by a snake. After more than a month with no sightings on any reserve in the Sabi Sands, it was accepted that she, along with her young litter, had perished.
leopards.territory: This female held a territory over eastern Marthly. A lack of roads in this area as well as her movements into our neighbours north and east of our property meant this was a leopard we did not see very regularly. Dense drainage lines and combretum woodlands also meant she often moved through this area unnoticed.

leopards.excerpt: The Tamboti female inhabited the south-eastern sections of Londolozi, having a large part of her territory along the Maxabene Riverbed.
leopards.profile: The Tamboti female was another of the Sunset Bend lineage that displayed the beautiful golden coat of her mother. Born on Londolozi in 2007, she moved east of our boundary after attaining independence, but in 2011 began moving back west and further south, pressurising the older females who were territorial at the time. Initially taking over the eastern areas of the Maxabene female’s territory, she eventually moved south to put pressure onto the Dudley Riverbank female, and came to dominate much of the south eastern section of the reserve, from Tsessebe clearing in the west down to Tshabalala Pan in the south, with the Sand River forming her eastern territorial boundary. Although female leopards can give birth from the age of three onwards, it took far longer than that for the Tamboti female to reproduce for the first time, and she was almost six years old when she finally had her first litter. Two cubs were born in early 2013, one of which survived and is territorial today. Two further litters were lost; one born in early 2015 and a second in late 2015, which was killed by the Dudley Riverbank 5:5 male in January of 2016. The Tamboti female spent a large amount of her timing hunting along the Maxabene riverbed, although sightings of her in the early parts of 2016 were fewer in number than in previous years. She was viewed with great consistency during the majority of 2017 and early 2018 during which time she was raising a young female, but the Tamboti female disappeared in the winter of 2018 after sustaining injuries in what was a suspected lion attack. The cub survived to independence.
leopards.territory: This leopard's territory falls predominantly in eastern Sparta and Dudley, with her using the Maxabene drainage line and Sand River for hunting opportunities and den sites. There is a distinct lack of rocky sections though, which may be one of the reasons she struggles to raise youngsters, and she has been seen using fallen root systems and aardvark holes as den sites instead.

leopards.excerpt: Londolozi's oldest territorial female. Distinguished by her nose spot, this Sunsetbend matriarch's legacy lives on through her daughters.
leopards.profile: Heritage & Lineage Born in September 2008 to the Vomba Female and sired by the Camp Pan Male, the Mashaba Female carries the distinctive golden coat characteristic of the Sunsetbend lineage. She represents one of the most successful branches of this prestigious bloodline at Londolozi. Territory Originally establishing herself around the Londolozi camps, her territory has shifted significantly over the years. In late 2018, she began moving southward, initially occupying the area left vacant by the deceased Tamboti Female. Currently, she holds territory in the area formerly occupied by the Tatowa Female, demonstrating the dynamic nature of leopard territorial behaviour. Physical Characteristics Distinctive spot in the pink of her nose Notable striations in her irises Classic 3:3 spot pattern Golden coat characteristic of the Sunsetbend lineage Reproductive History The Mashaba Female has shown remarkable persistence in reproduction, though faced with significant challenges. Her reproductive history includes: Successful Offspring: Nkoveni Female (August 2012) Ximungwe Female (May 2015) Notable Attempts: Twelve documented litters between 2012 and 2023, totalling more than 30 cubs Demonstrated exceptional resilience in continuing to reproduce despite numerous setbacks Current Status As of 2024, she holds the distinction of being Londolozi’s oldest territorial female. Despite her age, she continues to demonstrate remarkable resilience and adaptability, maintaining her territory and attempting to reproduce. Her successful offspring, particularly the Nkoveni and Ximungwe females, have themselves established territories and produced cubs, ensuring the continuation of her lineage. Behavioural Notes The Mashaba Female exemplifies the adaptability of leopards, having successfully adjusted her territory multiple times throughout her life in response to changing dynamics and pressure from other leopards. Her longevity and successful raising of two female cubs to independence have made her one of the most significant contributors to Londolozi’s current leopard population. Historical Significance Her life story spans a significant period in Londolozi’s leopard history. Through her daughters and their offspring, she has played a crucial role in maintaining the prestigious Sunsetbend lineage. Her bloodline continues to influence the leopard dynamics of the reserve, with her descendants now raising cubs of their own.
leopards.territory: The Mashaba female's territory is centred in the area around the Londolozi camps; she is an almost constant presence in the riverine bush and bushwillow-covered hillsides where she uses the drainage lines to move between key areas in her territory. The drainage lines which form a key part of her territory are also ideal hunting grounds for impala, bushbuck and nyala antelope which form a core component of her diet.

leopards.excerpt: Initially skittish female who transformed into a regular presence. Made history by raising first intact litter since her own generation.
leopards.profile: Heritage & Lineage Born in June 2011 to the Tutlwa Female and sired by the Marthly Male, she represents the continuing strength of the Sunsetbend lineage. Part of a litter of two, she and her brother (who later dispersed) were one of the rare examples of both cubs reaching independence successfully. Territory Currently maintains territory in northwestern Sparta and southwestern Marthly, spanning from the Londolozi Camps across to Singita. Her territory represents a portion of her mother’s former range, exemplifying the common practice of female leopards ceding territory to their daughters. This region includes significant portions of the Sand River system and its associated drainages. Physical Characteristics 3:2 spot pattern Distinctive pink nose with spots in it Currently notable limp on back left leg Reproductive History The Nhlanguleni Female has shown remarkable persistence in her reproductive efforts: Successful Offspring: March 2018: Nkuwa Female and Finfoot Female (first intact litter successfully raised since her own generation) Notable Attempts: November 2015: Two cubs denned in Sand River (litter lost) October 2017: One cub denned in Sand River (litter lost) March 2018: Intact litter raised- Nkuwa Female and Finfoot Female Mid-late 2019: Two cubs denned in Sand River (litter lost) January 2020: Two cubs denned at Mhangeni Double Crossing (litter lost) August 2020: One cub denned in Sand River (litter lost) March 2022: Two cubs denned in Sand River then Mhangeni Double Crossing (litter lost) January 2023: One cub seen at Mhangeni Double Crossing (litter lost) June 2023: Two cubs at Mhangeni Double Crossing (lost to hyenas) August 2024: Cub moved to Mhangeni Double Crossing (litter lost) Current Status Maintains a presence in her territory despite now suffering from a significant limp in her back left leg. Despite this physical challenge, she continues to demonstrate reproductive persistence after numerous setbacks. Her successful raising of the Nkuwa and Finfoot Females remains a significant achievement in recent Londolozi leopard history. Behavioural Notes Her journey from a skittish, rarely-seen leopard to a regularly viewed individual is a testament to the patience of Londolozi’s tracking team. Only beginning to relax around vehicles in 2015 at age 4, her transformation can be attributed to the consistent, sensitive viewing practices employed by guides and trackers. Her early years spent in the relatively inaccessible sections of the Sand River shaped her initial wary nature. Historical Significance The Nhlanguleni Female’s successful raising of an intact litter (Nkuwa and Finfoot females) marks a significant milestone, being the first time this had been achieved since her own generation. This success has particular importance for the continuation of the Sunsetbend lineage, with her daughter the Nkuwa Female now establishing herself as a territorial female in her own right. Her story demonstrates both the challenges and potential successes in leopard conservation, particularly regarding the habituation process and the importance of genetic continuity in the population.
leopards.territory: The Nhlanguleni female holds territory around north-west Sparta. Despite spending a majority of her time in the short grasslands of western Londolozi, she has been consistently shifting her territory further north and east to incorporate parts of the Sand River. This leopard particularly favours hunting and moving in the dense riverine bush making her difficult to find at times; her presence only known by the multitude of alarm calls that follow in her wake.

leopards.excerpt: Londolozi's most viewed leopard and prolific mother. This gorgeous female has raised multiple cubs to independence.
leopards.profile: Heritage & Lineage Born in August 2012 to the Mashaba Female and sired by the Marthly Male, she carries the prestigious Sunsetbend lineage. Born as part of a litter of two, though her sibling was only briefly seen in the early days before disappearing. Territory Currently maintains territory in northeastern Sparta, ranging from the Sand River south to Tamboti Donga. Following the successful raising of the Plaque Rock Female, she ceded her western territory to her daughter and shifted further east. Her current territory extends no further west than Warrens Road, with a significant presence in the marula crests near the eastern boundary. Reproductive History The Nkoveni Female has demonstrated both remarkable success and resilience through tragedy: Successful Offspring: March 2018: Plaque Rock Female February 2021: Xinkhova Female and Stone Drift Female (both reached independence) January 2024: Currently raising one surviving cub of a litter of three. Notable Attempts: Mid 2016: Two cubs (litter lost) January 2017: Two cubs denned at Trogon Dam (lost to Flat Rock Male) March 2018: One cub denned in Sand River- Plaque Rock Female February 2021: Two cubs denned in Mala Mala- Xinkhova and Stone Drift Females February 2023: Two cubs (killed by Three Rivers Female) January 2024: Three cubs denned in Mala Mala, one broke its jaw then killed by Kambula Pride at 4 months old, another killed at 10 months old by Kambula Pride. Current Status She is raising one young male cub from her January 2024 litter. She demonstrates incredible resilience after losing one cub to a jaw injury and recent dramatic encounters with the Kambula Pride. Despite facing significant challenges, she shows exceptional maternal care and hunting prowess. Behavioural Notes Her journey from a cautious cub to a confident adult is noteworthy. Initially isolated in her early months, she underwent a remarkable transformation at seven months of age, suddenly becoming notably relaxed around vehicles. She’s known for her comfort in marula trees and exceptional mothering skills, even showing remarkable attention to an injured cub before its eventual loss. Perhaps most notably, she recently demonstrated extraordinary courage and fighting spirit in protecting her cubs from a pride of lions, managing to escape a direct confrontation through quick thinking and agility. Though she lost one cub in this encounter, her survival instincts and maternal protection helped save her remaining cub. Historical Significance The Nkoveni Female represents the successful continuation of the Sunsetbend lineage through multiple generations. Her success in raising multiple female offspring to independence (Plaque Rock, Xinkhova, and Stone Drift females) has significantly contributed to the leopard population dynamics at Londolozi. Her story encompasses both the triumphs and tragedies that characterize the life of a female leopard in this environment, making her one of the most well-documented and followed leopards in recent Londolozi history.

Her male sibling disappeared at the age of around 4 months, but the Island female survived long enough to begin establishing her own territory at the end of 2015. She was independent relatively early on, making her first recorded kill at only 8 months old; a young impala lamb near Sunset Bend Clearing. As of early 2016 we are still unsure exactly where she will settle down, as the areas she is viewed in most often lie sandwiched between the territories of three other females; her mother, the Nkoveni female and the Ndzanzeni female. It is quite possible she will establish territory further east and sighting frequency could decline.

This area also has large, substantial trees that serve as ideal vantage points and hoisting sites.

leopards.excerpt: Golden-coated of Sunsetbend lineage, this female is gradually expanding her presence south of the Sand River into Londolozi.
leopards.profile: Named after the productive Piccadilly Triangle area in Mala Mala Heritage & Lineage Born in December 2013 to the Xidulu Female, the Piccadilly Female represents another branch of the prestigious Sunset bend lineage, evidenced by her distinctive golden coat. She was born in a litter of two females, both reaching independence – a notable achievement. Her sister, the Sibuye Female, established territory further north and east in Mala Mala. Territory Her territory has evolved significantly over time. Initially spending much time beyond Londolozi’s borders, she began exploiting opportunities created when the Nkoveni Female shifted east, establishing a presence along the southern bank of the Sand River and occasionally north towards the Manyelethi. Recently, she’s been seen more frequently just south of the Sand River, east of the Londolozi Camps – territory previously held by the late Plaque Rock Female. This area is currently contested, with the Xinkhova Female also showing interest in establishing herself there. Physical Characteristics Distinctive 3:3 spot pattern Pink nose Golden coat characteristic of the Sunset bend lineage Reproductive History The Piccadilly Female has shown increasing success in her reproductive efforts: Successful Offspring: April 2020: Ngungwe Female (viewable on Marthly) Mid 2023: Matumi Male (currently within mother’s territory) Notable Attempts: Mid 2019: One cub (litter lost) April 2020: Ngungwe Female January 2023: Two cubs denned near Stwise (litter lost) Mid 2023: Matumi Male Current Status Currently maintaining territory while raising the Matumi Male. Her movements between Londolozi and Mala Mala demonstrate the fluid nature of leopard territories, particularly in border areas. She faces potential territorial pressure from the Xinkhova Female in areas previously controlled by the Plaque Rock Female. Behavioural Notes Despite not being frequently viewed on Londolozi historically, she has shown remarkable adaptability in utilizing territorial opportunities. Her success in raising cubs to independence suggests she’s found a balance between the different reserves she frequents. Like many leopards of the Sunset Bend lineage, she’s proven to be an attentive mother, successfully raising offspring despite the challenges of a territory spanning multiple reserves. Historical Significance The Piccadilly Female represents an important extension of the Sunset Bend lineage, successfully establishing herself across reserve boundaries. Through her daughter, the Ngungwe Female, she’s contributed to the continuation of this prestigious bloodline, while her current success with the Matumi Male demonstrates her ongoing contribution to the leopard population. Her territorial movements provide valuable insights into how leopards adapt to changing dynamics and opportunities in neighbouring reserves.

Her territory extends from the Manyelethi/Sand RIver confluence, north past Stwise koppies towards the Marthly/Marthly boundary. The majority of her territory is on Mala Mala.

Territory Maintains a strong presence in central Londolozi, having inherited much of her territory from her mother, the Mashaba Female. Her range extends through the central parts of Sparta, an area she’s successfully defended since independence. The proximity of her territory to camp has made her one of Londolozi’s most frequently viewed leopards. Physical Characteristics 5:3 spot pattern Golden coat characteristic of the Sunsetbend lineage Notably relaxed around vehicles since an early age Reproductive History The Ximungwe Female has proven to be an exceptionally successful mother: Successful Offspring: October 2018: Mahlahla Male (female sibling killed by Tortoise Pan Male at 7 months) February 2021: Ntomi Male (only one cub ever seen) Notable attempts: December 2023: Two cubs born in Schwein Donga, killed by hyenas at 3/4 months old October 2024: One cub denned off Warthog skull, is currently still alive. Current Status Currently raising her third litter of cubs, demonstrating once again her exceptional maternal skills. She continues to be one of Londolozi’s most viewed leopards, though known for occasional periods of extended absence, particularly when denning cubs. Behavioural Notes She is known for her exceptional hunting prowess, particularly during adverse weather conditions. Her comfort around vehicles, established from an early age, has allowed for unprecedented viewing opportunities of natural leopard behaviour. She displays an interesting pattern of periodically “disappearing” for weeks at a time, often coinciding with pregnancy or early denning periods. A notably strategic mother, she carefully selects den sites and demonstrates excellent judgment in moving cubs when necessary. Her most recent den site selection in December 2023 showed her experienced approach to motherhood, choosing a well-protected boulder cluster that had previously proven successful for other females. Historical Significance The Ximungwe Female represents the successful continuation of the Sunsetbend lineage’s presence in central Londolozi. Her remarkable success rate in raising cubs to independence – particularly male cubs – is noteworthy, as young males typically face greater challenges surviving to adulthood. Her contribution to the leopard population extends beyond Londolozi’s boundaries, with her sons establishing territories in neighbouring areas.

leopards.profile: Named after the confluence of the Three Major Rivers on Mala Mala. Heritage & Lineage Born in May 2016 to the Xidulu Female and sired by the Piva Male, part of the Sunsetbend lineage. Her early life was marked by tragedy when her mother was killed by the Avoca male lions when she was just 11 months old. Her male sibling disappeared shortly afterwards. Territory Currently maintains territory in southeastern Londolozi, characterized by beautiful tamboti thickets, marshes, and open grasslands. Her territory has evolved through recent conflicts, particularly with the Nkoveni Female, leading to some territorial adjustments. She’s known to utilize the area from the Sand River south to the Maxabene riverbed. Physical Characteristics 2:2 spot pattern Notably small frame for an adult female Athletic build despite her size Distinctive pink nose and narrow muzzle Reproductive History Has shown remarkable resilience in her reproductive efforts: Successful Offspring: July 2021: Nsuku Male (raised to independence, sibling lost at 4 months) March 2024: Currently raising one cub (sibling lost) Notable Attempts: July 2021: Two cubs denned in Mala Mala. One lost at 4 months old. The remaining cub survived- Nsuku Male April 2023: Seen with suckle-marks, litter lost. November 2023: Litter lost March 2024: Two cubs denned in Mala Mala. Young Female still alive. Current Status Currently raising a single three-month-old cub after losing its sibling. Despite recent territorial conflicts with the Nkoveni Female that resulted in severe injuries, she has shown remarkable recovery and continues to demonstrate excellent maternal care. Behavioural Notes Despite her small size, she’s proven to be an exceptionally capable hunter, often taking down prey significantly larger than herself. She displays remarkable resilience, having recovered from severe injuries sustained in territorial disputes, particularly the dramatic 2023 conflict with the Nkoveni Female. Her territory presents unique challenges, including the regular presence of the Kambula Pride and Ndzhenga Males, territorial pressure from the Nkoveni Female and Xinkhova Female, and the presence of nomadic males. Despite these challenges, she continues to adapt and thrive. Historical Significance The Three Rivers Female represents one of Londolozi’s most remarkable survival stories. Forced into independence at an unusually young age, she has defied expectations to become a successful territorial female. Her resilience in the face of numerous challenges – from early orphaning to territorial conflicts and the challenges of raising cubs – makes her one of Londolozi’s most inspiring leopard stories.

leopards.title: Finfoot 3:3 Female
leopards.name: Finfoot
leopards.excerpt: A daughter of the Nhlanguleni female, born into a litter of two, both of which survived to independence.
leopards.profile: In early 2018 the Nhlanguleni female gave birth to a litter of two females. Kept well hidden at various dens along the Mhangeni drainage during their formative months, as well as in the Sand River itself, both these cubs nevertheless grew up relatively relaxed around the Land Rovers. Both females were raised to independence; the first time an intact litter had been successfully raised since the litter their mother was part of 7 years prior. Upon reaching independence, the sisters were regularly encountered in close proximity to one another, sometimes even feeding off the same kills. Towards late 2019 they began splitting up, with one female (renamed the Nkuwa female) spending the majority of her time further west in her mother’s territory, and the Finfoot female (so named because of the number of times she was encountered near Finfoot Crossing) spending the majority of her time in the eastern sector of her mother’s territory, much closer to the Londolozi camps. During 2020, this female was seen along the fenceline in southern Sabi Sabi nearing the Paul Kruger Gate. Seeking out a territory further afield.

leopards.profile: Named after the Shangaan word for Sycamore Fig trees which dot her territory along the Sand River Heritage & Lineage Born in March 2018 to the Nhlanguleni Female and sired by the Anderson Male, she carries the prestigious Sunsetbend lineage. She was born in a historical litter – with her sister the Finfoot Female, they were the first intact litter to reach independence since their mother’s own generation in 2012. Territory Maintains territory in northwestern Londolozi, primarily in western Sparta south of the Sand River, extending north along the Marthly/Othawa boundary. Her territory significantly overlaps with her mother’s, though she has established dominance in the western portions. The area is characterized by dense vegetation along the riverbanks and prominent Sycamore Fig trees. Physical Characteristics 3:3 spot pattern Distinctive bright pink nose Facial features characteristic of the Sunsetbend lineage Reproductive History Has shown increasing success in her reproductive efforts: Successful Offspring: February 2023: Two male cubs (2:2 and 3:3 spot patterns) successfully raised to independence Previous Attempts: The first litter lost at a few months old Currently seen mating with Ntomi Male and Thamba Male, suggesting potential pregnancy Current Status At six years old, she has proven herself as a capable mother after successfully raising two male cubs to independence – a rare achievement at Londolozi. Behavioural Notes Demonstrates similar secretive denning behaviour to her mother, often keeping cubs well hidden during their early months. Shows exceptional hunting abilities, particularly important during the demanding period of raising two male cubs. Her success in raising both male cubs to independence, despite the increased nutritional demands, speaks to her hunting prowess and maternal capability. Historical Significance The Nkuwa Female represents a significant success story in the continuation of the Sunsetbend lineage. Her achievement in raising two male cubs to independence is particularly noteworthy, as it’s relatively rare for both cubs in a litter to survive, especially males. Her overlapping territory with her mother, the Nhlanguleni Female, provides an interesting study in mother-daughter dynamics among Londolozi’s leopards.

leopards.excerpt: Born 2018, skilled huntress and determined mother. Dominated Sand River territory until her tragic end in 2024.
leopards.profile: Named after the iconic ‘Plaque Rock’ along the banks of the Sand River, a place of high significance to the Varty family, it bears three plaques in remembrance of Charles Boyd Varty, Maidie Varty and Howard Mackie. Heritage & Lineage Born in March 2018 to the Nkoveni Female, the Plaque Rock Female represented a significant milestone as her mother’s first successfully raised offspring. Her birth marked a new chapter in the prestigious Sunsetbend lineage, connecting her through her grandmother, the Mashaba Female, to one of Londolozi’s most celebrated leopard dynasties. Raised in the productive areas around the Sand River, she grew up remarkably relaxed around vehicles, a trait inherited from both her mother and grandmother. Territory Her territory acquisition tells a story of careful maternal planning. As she approached independence, her mother, the Nkoveni Female, began a gradual shift eastward, effectively ceding prime river territory to her daughter. The Plaque Rock Female established herself in an ideal location that included the Sand River’s eastern sections near Londolozi camps, creating a perfect base for both hunting and future denning sites. This territory offered everything a female leopard could desire – access to water, abundant prey, and numerous secure locations for raising cubs. The complex network of drainage lines and granite boulder clusters would later prove crucial in her own attempts at motherhood. Physical Characteristics Like her mother, she carried the 2:2 spot pattern that would later be shared by her sister, the Xinkhova Female. Distinctive pink nose Reproductive History The Plaque Rock Female’s story as a mother reflects both the harsh realities and profound determination of leopard motherhood. Though she never successfully raised cubs to independence, each attempt revealed her growing experience and maternal instincts: First Litter (2022): Cubs were lost before they could be viewed Second Litter (2022): Briefly seen before disappearing in the challenging summer months Third Litter (2023-2024): Her most successful attempt, giving birth to three cubs which she moved between multiple den sites, showing remarkable maternal care before their tragic loss Final Litter (2024): Had just revealed a single cub to the world before her untimely death Behavioural Notes Her character was marked by a playful spirit that never quite faded even as she matured into a formidable hunter. She showed particular skill in hunting kudu calves and impala, regularly utilizing the riverine vegetation for cover. Her comfort around vehicles allowed for intimate observations of her behaviour, from playful tree-climbing sessions to tender moments with her cubs. Perhaps most remarkably, she maintained an unusual tolerance of her mother’s presence, often allowing relatively close proximity without the typical aggression shown between territorial females. Final Chapter The Plaque Rock Female’s life came to a tragic end in June 2024, during an encounter with the Ntsevu Pride and Ndzhenga Males in the Sand River on Mala Mala. At just six years old, her passing marked the end of a short but impactful presence in Londolozi’s leopard population. The vacancy left in her territory opened the possibility for her sister, the Xinkhova Female, to establish herself in this prime location, potentially continuing the family’s legacy along the Sand River. Historical Significance Though her time was cut short, the Plaque Rock Female’s legacy lives on through the stories of those who witnessed her journey. She demonstrated the successful inheritance of territory from mother to daughter, showed remarkable resilience in the face of reproductive challenges, and maintained the prestigious Sunsetbend lineage’s presence along the Sand River. Her life, though tragically brief, embodied the complex dynamics of leopard society at Londolozi, from territorial relationships to the challenges of motherhood in this unforgiving environment.

Her choice of den site in the rocky outcrops of Marthly Pools demonstrates sound maternal instincts. Historical Significance This represents an interesting case study in leopard habituation, showing how even an initially skittish leopard can develop comfort around vehicles through patient viewing practices. As the daughter of the Piccadilly Female, she maintains the prestigious Sunsetbend lineage in the central portions of Marthly, and her recent transition to motherhood marks an important continuation of this bloodline.
