During their dependent years, she and her sister were frequently seen sharing kills even after reaching independence, an unusual behaviour that demonstrated their strong sibling bond. Her successful transition to independence and quick establishment of territory speaks to her capabilities as a young leopard. Her quick transition to motherhood and successful territory establishment suggests she will play a significant role in maintaining the strength of the Sunsetbend lineage in the greater Sabi Sands area, even if primarily viewed on neighbouring properties.

Historical Significance This represents an important continuation of the Nkoveni Female’s lineage and potentially the next generation of dominant females at Londolozi. Her establishment in the former Plaque Rock Female’s territory would maintain a family presence in this prime area, while her comfort around vehicles suggests potential for excellent viewing opportunities in coming years. Her journey provides fascinating insights into how young female leopards navigate territorial establishment in a landscape dense with established leopards.

leopards.title: Shingi 3:3 Male
leopards.name: Shingi
leopards.excerpt: The last surviving cub of a litter of three, he is on the cusp of independence.
leopards.profile: Recently independent, he has been named after the prominent waterhole in the southeast, Shingi Dam. Heritage & Lineage Born in January 2024 to the Nkoveni 2:2 Female and sired by the Maxim’s Male, the Nkoveni Young Male represents the merging of two powerful leopard lineages. His mother is one of Londolozi’s most prolific and well-known females, descended from the Mashaba Female and Marthly Male of the Sunsetbend bloodline. His father, the Maxim’s Male, is currently the dominant male across much of the southern Sabi Sands and is known for his impressive size, power, and success. He was born into a litter of three—two sisters and himself. Tragically, both of his sisters were lost to the Kambula Pride in separate incidents, leaving him as the sole survivor of the litter. This is the first time the Nkoveni Female has successfully raised a male cub to this age, making his development particularly significant. Developmental Stage & Independence Now approximately 18 months old, the Nkoveni Young Male is at the brink of full independence. While he continues to share kills with his mother on occasion, his behaviour increasingly reflects the hallmarks of an emerging solitary male: prolonged solo forays, bold exploration, and frequent tree-climbing displays. He has become notably dominant around food, often denying his mother access to kills she has made. This behaviour is more typical of established adult males and highlights his accelerating maturity. On multiple occasions, he has hoisted kills into trees, growled his mother away, and shown reluctance to share—behaviour that is not typically expected from a cub still under maternal care. His physical development has kept pace: he now rivals his mother in size and is rapidly growing in muscle and confidence. The coming months will likely see him pushed further afield, and the extent to which his father, the Maxim’s Male, tolerates his presence will heavily influence the timing and direction of this next phase. Physical Characteristics 3:3 spot pattern Muscular frame for his age, with a developing thick neck and broad chest Golden coat with rich rosettes that reflect his father’s impressive genetics Expressive amber eyes, slightly softer features compared to other males of similar age Behavioural Notes The Nkoveni Young Male displays a growing self-assurance nurtured by the security of his mother’s territory and her attentive guidance. While he was once the least confident of his litter, he has evolved into a bold and dominant young leopard. He has repeatedly been observed asserting control over kills, hoisting and guarding them even from his mother and, in one remarkable instance, standing his ground against the Maxim’s Male. Though the larger male eventually redirected his attention to the Nkoveni Female, the young male’s audacity signalled a readiness to challenge dominance far earlier than expected. Still, his inexperience remains evident. He retreats into trees at the approach of hyenas and exhibits a learning curve in refining hunting and defensive strategies. Despite this, his play, curiosity, and physical boldness are unmistakable signs of his emergence as a force in the making. Territorial Outlook Like all young males, the Nkoveni Young Male will soon embark on a nomadic phase. He will likely spend the next year or two wandering the reserve and beyond, avoiding dominant males while developing the skills and strength needed to one day compete for a territory of his own. Initially, his movements are expected to orbit the outer reaches of his mother’s territory, particularly near productive hunting areas like Shingilana Dam. The timing of his final departure will depend on food availability, his confidence, and most significantly, the tolerance of his father, the Maxim’s Male. Significance and Legacy The Nkoveni Young Male is an important emerging figure in the continuing story of the Sunsetbend lineage. He represents both the resilience of his mother—who survived the loss of two cubs and a brutal encounter with lions—and the genetic strength of his dominant father. He is poised to take his place as a future force in the Londolozi leopard landscape, provided he can navigate the complex and often perilous nomadic chapter ahead. In his journey, we see echoes of those who came before him: the survival instincts of the Nkoveni Female, the dominance of the Maxim’s Male, and the mysterious and ancient rhythm that guides all young male leopards as they step out into the wild to find their future. If his recent behaviour is anything to go by, he will not go quietly, he is a leopard with presence, power, and a future worth watching closely.

leopards.title: Tinxiya 4:3 Female
leopards.name: Tinxiya
leopards.excerpt: A confident and curious young leopard, that is nearing independence after a remarkable start to life alongside her resilient mother.
leopards.profile: Recently independent, she has been named after the Shangaan word tinxiya, meaning eyebrows. This is in relation to her particularly long eyebrow lashes when she was young ,and now the prominent eyebrow ridge she has inherited from her father. Heritage & Lineage Born in March 2024 to the Three Rivers 2:2 Female and sired by the Maxim’s Male, the Three Rivers Young Female represents the next generation in a legendary bloodline. Her mother, descended from the Piva Male and Xidulu Female, is known for her resilience and success despite early orphaning. Her father, the Maxim’s Male, is arguably one of the largest and most dominant male leopards in the Sabi Sand Reserve. The young female bears a striking resemblance to him, both in her robust build and in the confident, assured way she carries herself. Though she was born into a litter of two, only she has survived; her sibling lost early. Territorial Development Still partially dependent on her mother, the Three Rivers Young Female is entering the exploratory phase of adolescence. She is frequently seen alongside her mother at kills, yet sightings also show her venturing into surrounding areas with increasing independence. It is anticipated that she will soon be fully independent and forced to establish a territory of her own. Her future territorial prospects remain uncertain. Her mother’s territory, positioned in the southeastern sector of Londolozi, lies at the convergence of several other female territories, such as the Nkoveni, Xinkhova, Ximungwe, and Ndzanzeni Females. This makes for a highly contested environment. While it is possible that the Three Rivers Female may cede part of her territory to her daughter (a common maternal behaviour), external pressures may drive the young female to seek space further afield, possibly across the Sand River into a less densely populated region. Physical Characteristics Compact, muscular frame Eyes reminiscent of her mother with the broad facial structure of her father Confident posture, often observed climbing and scanning her surroundings from elevated positions Development and Behaviour Displaying a balance of playfulness and growing maturity, the Three Rivers Young Female is often seen climbing trees, stalking small prey, and practising critical survival skills. Her relationship with her mother has begun to shift, with less grooming, more tolerance, indicating the early stages of separation. While she continues to benefit from her mother’s skills and presence, the signs of emerging independence are clear. Notably, she was recently seen with both her mother and the Maxim’s Male, an unusual sighting given the typically solitary nature of leopards and the male’s tendency to remain aloof. In a rare moment, she was observed playfully interacting with the male, suggesting an extraordinary degree of tolerance on his part. These interactions offer a unique glimpse into her social development and the bonds that may have helped safeguard her early life. Current Status Now around 17 months old, the Three Rivers Young Female is approaching the threshold of independence. Her presence still overlaps heavily with her mother’s, but she is slowly carving out her own narrative. The next few months will likely see her establishing a more defined range and refining her hunting and territorial skills. As she matures, the resilience and adaptability she inherits from her lineage will be crucial in determining her success. Significance and Legacy The Three Rivers Young Female represents the continuing arc of one of Londolozi’s most iconic lineages. Her mother, the Three Rivers Female, was herself orphaned at a young age but managed to establish territory and successfully raise cubs. Her father is a powerful force across the reserve. Now, as their daughter nears independence, she carries forward not only their genetic strength but also the hopes of continuing a story that began with the legendary Mother Leopard over four decades ago.
leopards.territory: Not yet territorial. See in the southeastern parts of Londolozi and Dudley. From Princess Alice's Pans all the way down to Tshabalala Pan.

leopards.name: Camp Pan
leopards.death_note: Unknown
leopards.excerpt: The King of Londolozi in his day; an enormous male whose offspring still inhabit the reserve.
leopards.profile: One of the true legends of the Leopards of Londolozi, the Camp Pan male was dominant over a significant portion of the property for a good six years, longer than the average tenure expected of a male leopard in a hotly contested environment like the Sabi Sands. Born in 2000 to the Tavangumi female, he spent a great deal of time around Singita’s Camp Pan during his formative months, which is where he got his name. In 2007 he began pushing east into Londolozi and established himself almost overnight, pushing out the dominant Sparta 5:5 male in the process. His territory was enormous, stretching from the Manyelethi River in the north to beyond the Maxabene River in the South. With the arrival of the Marthly male in 2010, the Camp Pan male was forced to start ceding territory in the north while consolidating territory in the south, but he was slowly but surely forced further and further south and east, eventually getting ousted altogether by the Piva male pushing in from the opposite direction. The Camp Pan male had an interesting relationship with one of his sons, the Tu-Tones male, with whom he almost shared territory, tolerating his presence and not forcing him out as most males would their sons. The two males would be seen on the same kills and even mating with the same female at the same time. During his reign the Camp Pan male fathered a number of eminently viewable leopards, including the Tutlwa and Mashaba females, ensuring that his legacy lives on. He was last seen in the Spring of 2015.
leopards.territory: The Camp Pan male occupied territory in most of Sparta and Marthly during his initial phase of maturity. As he grew older, his territory was pushed progressively south and east into Dudley before he finally lost control of even this area under sustained pressure from the Piva male, becoming nomadic in late 2014.

leopards.title: Saseka 3:4 Female
leopards.name: Saseka
leopards.excerpt: Saseke was a dominant female who controlled territory over most of elephant plains in the north.
leopards.profile: Saseka was a dominant female who controlled territory over most of elephant plains in the north, westward into Othawa, the western portion of Simbambili and the north western portion of Arathusa Private Game Reserve. Her major competitors were the Safari female to the east (female with one blue eye), Nyelethi female (her daughter to the south) and unknown females in the west (Othawa). She was by far one of the most relaxed leopards in the northern sector and was photographed extensively by ODP photographic tours, who would photograph her almost exclusively. As a result she appears in the books “game drive” and “Greater Kruger- The Big Picture” by the Van den bergs. Her main ID characteristics were a 3:3 spot pattern and she had a slight kink in her right ear. She is estimated to have been born around 1995, but where she came from is only speculation. She raised at least two sets of cubs successfully. The Nyelethi 4:4 female, born 14 January 2003 (sired by Mafufnyane male) was raised to independence and moved south into Marthly. The female referred to as “Salayeshe” was born in the next litter. Salayeshe had a sibling which was presumed to have been killed by a hyena. She was raised to independence and when Saseke disappeared around 2008, Salayeshe “inherited” her territory. No one knows how Saseke died, she was last seen close to the Othawa break and was never seen again after that.
leopards.territory: This female's territory touched a tiny portion of Londolozi in northern Marthly.

leopards.title: Marthly 3:2 Male
leopards.name: Marthly
leopards.excerpt: This male moved in from the north of the reserve in 2010, and was instantly recognisable by his unique tuft of fur at the back of his neck.
leopards.profile: This unmistakeable male began being viewed more regularly from 2010 onwards, pushing in from the north of the reserve and forcing the dominant Camp Pan male out. His characteristic mane and notched right ear were easily recognisable. Almost immediately upon his encroachment into the territories of the females along the river, they all began falling pregnant, providing further evidence to support the theory that the ageing Camp Pan male may have become infertile in his old age. The Marthly male quickly established himself as the dominant male along the Sand River towards the end of 2011, and the Camp Pan male was forced further south. Towards the end of 2012 the slightly younger Gowrie male began encroaching from the north, forcing the Marthly male to consolidate his territory along an east-west line through the centre of the Marthly property. Venturing as far south as the Maxabene river, the territory was still large enough to allow for adequate mating access to females. By mid-2014 however, the Marthly male was hardly ever viewed north bank of the Sand River, yet he continued to be be active between the Maxabene and Londolozi Camps. Caught between the newly arrived Piva and Inyathini males in the south and the 4:4 male to the west, the Marthly male was eventually forced out of his territory altogether, and was nomadic as of the beginning of 2015. Forced to keep a low profile, avoiding other big males in the area, his condition steadily deteriorated and he was viewed for the last time on Londolozi in winter of 2015, very undernourished and with a number of injuries. It is assumed that he died shortly after, as after one or two sightings on other properties, he was not seen again.
leopards.territory: This male found himself sandwiched between a number of other dominant males throughout his life but managed to hold territory in Marthly, along the Sand River and later northern Sparta. In his later years, he spent a great deal of time south of the Sand River and north of Main Road where there are a number of prominent termite mounds. He would use these as vantage points as well as easy spots to sit and stake out warthog burrows.

leopards.title: Ravenscourt 3:2 Female
leopards.name: Ravenscourt
leopards.death_note: Killed by Nyelethi 4:3 male
leopards.excerpt: A gorgeous golden female, this leopard spent much of her time around the Singita camps, and was even known to den cubs in the lodge.
leopards.profile: The Ravenscourt female established territory to the west of Londolozi, quickly becoming the mainstay of the leopard viewing on our neighbour, Singita’s, property. She was famous for denning her cubs in or around the rooms at Boulders Lodge, forcing the lodge to close a particular room while she was using it to stash her cubs. She was killed in a dramatic fight with the Nyelethi 4:3 male in 2014, in which she defended her surviving cub from his attack in the branches of a leadwood tree. Racing up the trunk, she leaped outwards, tackling the Nyelethi male out of the fork, and the two plummeted to the ground. In the ensuing scuffle, she was bitten on the back of the neck and died instantly. Her cub survived, and established territory on Singita where he is known as the Ravenscout male.
leopards.territory: This leopard held territory to the west of Londolozi, south of the Sand River on Ravenscourt.

leopards.title: Emsagwen 4:6 Male
leopards.name: Emsagwen
leopards.death_note: Suggested to have been killed by a pride of lions.
leopards.excerpt: One of the bigger male leopards seen on Londolozi in recent years, the Emsagwen male wasn’t often encountered.
leopards.profile: One of the bigger male leopards seen on Londolozi in recent years, the Emsagwen male wasn’t often encountered, since most of his territory fell outside our borders. He was occasionally seen in the NE reaches of Londolozi, but sightings were infrequent at best. He was initially unrelaxed around vehicles, and it is therefore assumed that he originated in the Kruger National Park. His initial territory lay along the eastern border of the Sabi Sands and Kruger. His disappearance in the latter parts of 2011 remains a mystery, but there were some suggestions that he had met his fate at the hands of a pride of lions. His death left a territory vacant, and the Dudley Riverbank 5:5 male, who was battling for territory with the Camp Pan male at the time, moved across to fill the gap, granting the Camp Pan male a lifeline.
leopards.territory: This leopard was occasionally viewed in eastern Marthly, but the true extent of his territory was relatively unknown as most of it fell outside our borders.

leopards.title: Gowrie 2:2 Male
leopards.name: Gowrie
leopards.excerpt: The Gowrie male first appeared in the Sabi Sands around 2011. Judging by his size, he is estimated to have been born around 2005/6.
leopards.profile: The Gowrie male first appeared in the Sabi Sands around 2011, and was reportedly quite skittish. This makes it likely that he was born in the Kruger Park and grew up unused to vehicles. His dispersal into the private game reserve system as a young male meant he soon began being viewed regularly and began to relax around vehicles as a result. Judging by his size when he was first viewed, he is estimated to have been born around 2005/2006, although it is impossible to say for sure. As he moved into the northern parts of Londolozi in 2012, he began putting pressure on the dominant and much older Marthly male, who was forced to retreat slowly, conceding territory all the time and eventually being forced south of the Sand River altogether. The Gowrie male’s arrival was ill-timed as far as the local female population was concerned, as the Tutlwa and Ximpalapala females were raising litters at the time, both of which were believed to have been killed by the Gowrie male. The Gowrie male subsequently became dominant over the whole of Marthly, even being seen on the Southern bank of the river on a few occasions. Then, in mid-2015, sightings of him suddenly dried up. No tracks moved through the Manyelethi River and his territorial call was heard no more. Eventually it was accepted that he was dead, through causes unknown. A part of a leopard’s lower jaw was found in the Manyelethi riverbed near Marthly Pools, but as the displaced Marthly male had been seen in the area only a few months previously, it remains unclear who the jaw belonged to.
leopards.territory: This male established himself as the dominant male in the north of Londolozi on the section known as Marthly. He would move between the northern bank of the Sand River, with its profileration of game, through the rocky sections of central Marthly and through the seasonal Manyelethi River to our northern boundary. His territory had many females falling within it; a major drawing factor for a dominant male leopard.

leopards.title: Kaxane 3:3 Male
leopards.name: Kaxane
leopards.death_note: Old Age
leopards.excerpt: He was born to the Kapen female in 2005, and upon independence moved south the lower Sabi Sand.
leopards.profile: A male not often viewed on Londolozi, the Kaxane male (Kaxane means ‘far’ in Shangaan) is seen mainly in Singita and the western sectors of the reserve. He was born to the Kapen female of Mala Mala in 2005, and upon independence moved south into Sabi Sabi. He then began pushing north and westwards, establishing territory on the Castleton and Savannah properties towards the end of 2009. This male has very distinctive rich green eyes and a conspicuous notch in his right ear.
leopards.territory: The Kaxane male is occasionally viewed near Londolozi's western boundary. He holds a large and desirable territory in central Castleton and onto Ravenscourt.

leopards.title: Little Bush 3:3 Female
leopards.name: Little Bush
leopards.death_note: Killed by Mhangeni Pride Breakaway sub-adult lions

litters.description: Male cub killed by Mhangeni male. Female cub survived.
One cub disappeared at around four months. Female cubs till alive as of June 2016

leopards.excerpt: The Little Bush female is a rare visitor to Londolozi as most of her territory lies beyond our southern borders.
leopards.profile: The Little Bush female is a rare visitor to Londolozi as most of her territory lies beyond our southern borders. She is occasionally encountered in the deep south west around Makhotini and Vertical Dams, although the long grass of the area is not conducive to easy leopard finding. Notable sightings of her include August 2014, when she was viewed with a cub in the enormous sycamore fig tree near Makhotini dam, and then in June 2015 when she was found in company with the Warthog Wallow female (also from beyond our southern borders), both of them trailing the Makhotini male, who was ignoring both females, opting to hunt warthogs instead, one of which he successfully caught. The last recorded sighting of her on Londolozi soil was in mid-2015, when she was found with her female cub (the Kigelia female) off Handpump Road with a reedbuck kill which the Makhotini male had stolen from.
leopards.territory: This female holds a territory in the grasslands of south west Dudley. Within her territory lie a few very large Sycamore figs. Because of the open nature of the terrain, these trees serve as important training spots for her cubs to learn to climb in and noteable sightings include seeing them in the enormous boughs.

leopards.title: Anderson 4:4 Male
leopards.name: Anderson
leopards.death_note: Seen in very poor condition in the Sand River off the Causeway, robbed by Ntsevu Pride
leopards.excerpt: Unofficially the biggest leopard in the Sabi Sands, the Anderson male is an absolutely enormous individual in north western Londolozi.
leopards.profile: One of the biggest leopards in the Sabi Sands, the Anderson male is an absolutely enormous individual who is seen in the north western sections of Londolozi, from Ximpalapala koppie up to the northern break. After the death of the Marthly male, he has been seen to push further south and eastwards, and although being seen more regularly, is not 100% relaxed around vehicles yet. Although viewed occasionally in 2014, it was only upon the disappearance of the Marthly male that sightings of the Anderson male started becoming more frequent. He was seen mating with the Nanga female in April and May 2016, the female having lost a young litter of cubs shortly before that. Born in 2008, the Andreson male should still hopefully have many years left in him, and it is likely that his size will keep him firmly established in his area for some time to come.
leopards.territory: This leopard's territory falls into north western Marthly and has progressively been stretching further south and east into Londolozi. He is predominantly seen around the Ximpalapala Koppies, an ideal vantage point or even hunting spot for the rarely seen Klipspringer. Being such a large male, it is likely he is attempting to extend his territory further south to include the hotly contested Sand River, although he has not been recorded this far south yet.

leopards.title: Ingrid Dam 4:4 Female
leopards.name: Ingrid Dam

litters.description: Seen once playing with a pangolin

leopards.excerpt: She is occasionally seen around the far north west corner of Londolozi, and is generally quite relaxed around vehicles.
leopards.profile: We know very little about this leopard. She is occasionally seen around the far north-west corner of Londolozi, and is generally quite relaxed around vehicles, which is surprising as her contact with people is necessarily limited. Her symmetrical 4:4 spot pattern is unmistakeable; a row of three spots on each cheek with a fourth directly above it. In late 2014 she was seen to have suckle marks, indicating she was stashing cubs somewhere, and then in March 2015 she was found on our western boundary with a single cub of about 6-7 months, and both of them were playing with a pangolin. Since that sighting she has been viewed only once or twice. As properties to the north of Londolozi also know so little about this female it is presumed she spends much of her time to the west of us on the Othawa property, which does not see a lot of vehicle traffic. It is presumed that she spent her first year or two being viewed by Land Rovers, hence her relaxed demeanour. Her territory borders that of the much older Ximpalapala female, and it is quite possible that she is a daughter of this leopard.
leopards.territory: This leopard holds a small territory that includes a small portion of north western Marthly. This area is dominated by combretum and silver cluster leaf woodland, where kudu, duiker and nyala are prevalent.

leopards.title: Inyathini 3:3 Male
leopards.name: Inyathini
leopards.excerpt: Another leopard who originated in the Kruger National Park, he has established a large territory in the south eastern areas of Londolozi.
leopards.profile: Another leopard who originated in the Kruger National Park, this male was unrelaxed and even aggressive towards vehicles when first viewed on the Londolozi property, and charged a number of rangers during the early months of his tenure. After repeated viewings, he relaxed far more and sightings of him became far more consistent. He then established a large territory in the southeastern areas of Londolozi, from the Dudley Camp region along the Sand River to the eastern edge of the central grasslands. The area is relatively thick and tracking him proved to be difficult. He was believed to have fathered the Ndzanzeni Female’s male offspring, the Tortoise Pan Male. A serious territorial spat with the Piva male in winter of 2015 left both leopards cut up around the face and neck. As he has aged he has lost muscle mass, but is still being seen in the eastern parts of Dudley, along the Sand River. He has still been scent marking and calling as of February 2022 but no longer roams the enormous territory he used to.
leopards.territory: This leopard's territory falls mainly in eastern Dudley, with some of his favourite patrol routes and hunting spots falling around the Tugwaan Drainage. These areas provide ideal resting spots in the heavily shaded riverine bush, a high prey density as well as clean drinking water.

leopards.title: Robson’s 4:4 Male
leopards.name: Robson's
leopards.death_note: Mauled by Ntsevu Pride, died of wounds.
leopards.excerpt: This rangy male was an enigma, arriving on Londolozi in the mid to latter parts of 2014 and staying mainly in the western areas.
leopards.profile: This rangy male was rather an enigma, having arrived on Londolozi in the mid- to latter parts of 2014 and staying mainly in the western areas of the reserve, around the Sparta/Ravenscourt break and Mhangeni Donga. Sightings of a relatively unrelaxed male in the block south of Ximpalapala koppie from around the same time were also believed to be him. His skittish nature led us to suspect that he originated in the Kruger Park and grew up not being used to vehicles approaching him. First reports of this male were in the north of the Sabi Sands as a sub-adult in 2012. Since 2014 this male has expanded his territory massively, being found from beyond the Maxabene River in the south to the upper reaches of the Manyelethi River in the north, operating mainly in the western portions of Sparta. His territory is roughly the same size as the Camp Pan male’s once was, despite the 4:4 male being a significantly smaller animal. He was believed to be the father of the Mashaba young female and the February 2016 litter of the Nkoveni female. He was also seen in the company of the Nhlanguleni female and her cubs, and although she was seen mating with the Nyelethi male in the west in 2015, at least the 4:4 male believed himself to be the litter’s father. Sightings of this leopard were irregular at best, as he was reticent to patrol along roads, preferring to stay in drainage lines and thickets. When females in the area have kills hoisted, it was not uncommon to find the male feeding on the kill the next morning, having smelt it out during the night. In most sightings this leopard is nervous of more than two vehicles, but sometimes he relaxes tremendously for unknown reasons. We hope he relaxes more as sightings become more frequent.
leopards.territory: This leopard has a large territory that encompasses Sparta, predominantly north of the Maxabene all the way to central Marthly. Because this area is so large, he moves constantly and covers big distances in order to scent mark and patrol the area, thereby protecting it from potential male contenders.

leopards.title: Torchwood 3:3 Male
leopards.name: Torchwood
leopards.excerpt: The Torchwood male holds territory falling mostly to the west of Londolozi and is infrequently seen.
leopards.profile: The Torchwood Male is a young nomadic male that has drifted in from the north of the Sabi Sands in 2013. Born in November or December 2010 on the Torchwood property, he is now at an age at which his father would most likely have put pressure on him to move out of his territory. His father is the Mvula male (aka Leadwood Male) who is territorial to the north of us, and who we don’t see on Londolozi. Male leopards typically disperse at around two-and-a-half years, and this is mirrored exactly in the Torchwood male, as the last photo taken of him in the North was round about June 2013. Since then he has moved around the Sabi Sand extensively, being seen in the southern, western, and now central sectors. Currently the Torchwood male holds territory falling mostly to the west of Londolozi and is infrequently seen.
leopards.territory: The Torchwood Male is a young nomadic male that has drifted in from the north of the Sabi Sands in 2013.

leopards.title: Senegal Bush 3:3 Male
leopards.name: Senegal Bush
leopards.death_note: Unknown
leopards.excerpt: Dominant from 2019-2024, transformed from cautious visitor to powerful territorial force. Mastered central Londolozi until his final days.
leopards.profile: Named after an area in Mala Mala known as ‘Senegal Bush’ after a Senegalia senegal tree. Heritage & Lineage First viewed as a young male in 2016, after a short stint in the north he moved eastwards. Here he received his name and grew into a large dominant male. Territory Evolution His territory establishment followed several distinct phases: Initial Phase (2016): Brief appearances in northern Londolozi around Mahlahla Dam Eastern Phase (2017-2019): Established in eastern Marthly and Mala Mala Expansion Phase (2019): Pushed westward, displacing the ageing Inyathini Male Prime Period (2020-2023): Dominated central Londolozi from Mala Mala to central Sparta Final Phase (2023-2024): Gradually shifted northwestward under pressure from Maxims Male Physical Characteristics 3:3 spot pattern Distinctive deeply set eyes with a dark eyeliner that gave an intense stare Tattered ears from territorial conflicts Notable scars accumulated through years of territorial defence Behavioural Notes The Senegal Bush Male’s story is one of strategic territory acquisition and maintenance. Initially spotted making brief forays into Londolozi, he showed remarkable patience in establishing himself, choosing his moments carefully before making decisive moves to claim territory. His hunting prowess was particularly notable, showing exceptional skill with warthog hunting, often successfully ambushing them at their burrows. His territorial strategy was methodical and effective, using drainage lines and river systems to navigate his vast domain. He demonstrated remarkable tolerance of certain young males, particularly those likely to be his offspring, allowing them to feed from his kills – behaviour that proved crucial in establishing his genetic legacy in the area. Perhaps most remarkably, he maintained complex relationships with several females across his territory, successfully mating with the Nhlanguleni, Nkuwa, and Three Rivers females among others. His success in protecting these females’ territories and allowing his offspring to flourish demonstrated an impressive understanding of prime real estate. Final Chapter Last seen in June 2024, the Senegal Bush Male’s disappearance marked the end of a significant era in Londolozi’s leopard dynamics. Though his fate remains uncertain, his legacy continues through multiple offspring, including the Ntomi Male, who shows signs of following in his father’s footsteps. Historical Significance His impact on Londolozi’s leopard population extends far beyond his territorial reign: Successfully established and maintained prime territory through strategic expansion Contributed significantly to genetic diversity through multiple successful offspring Demonstrated exceptional parental tolerance, allowing likely offspring to share kills Showed remarkable adaptability in territory defence and expansion Left a lasting legacy through multiple offspring who continue to shape Londolozi’s leopard dynamics The Senegal Bush Male’s story embodies the complex dynamics of male leopard society, from initial establishment through territorial dominance to eventual succession. His influence continues through his offspring, who now shape the next chapter of Londolozi’s leopard population.
leopards.territory: The Senegal Bush male occupies a relatively central and narrow territory on Londolozi, with the Maxabene roughly marking the northern extent of it and the Sparta/Dudley boundary the southern end.

leopards.title: Flat Rock 3:2 Male
leopards.name: Flat Rock
leopards.excerpt: Born 2013 Kruger, seized prime territory at young age. Strategic dominance led to successful lineage before current eastward shift.
leopards.profile: Named after the Flat Rock area on the Tinga concession where he originated Heritage & Lineage Born in 2013 to the Porcupine Female and Mbavala Male on Tinga concession in Kruger National Park. His arrival at Londolozi in late 2016 coincided fortuitously with the death of the Robson’s 4:4 Male, allowing him to establish prime territory despite being only three years old. Territory Evolution His territory has developed in distinct phases: Initial Phase (2016): Small territory west of Londolozi camps, south of Sand River Expansion Phase (2017-2019): Extended east along the southern bank of Sand River Peak Domain (2019-2022): Controlled approximately 30 square kilometres, including: South of Sand River to Maxabene Northern sections across Marthly Prime river frontage and drainage systems Current Phase (2023-Present): Shifting further east and north under pressure from younger males Physical Characteristics 3:2 spot pattern Triangle of spots on the right side of the face Broad, impressive facial structure Notably large for young age during territory establishment Presumed Offspring Successfully sired multiple offspring through strategic territory defence: Plaque Rock Female (deceased) Nkuwa and Finfoot Females (first intact litter raised to independence since 2012) Likely father of recent litters from Ingrid Dam, Piccadilly, Mashaba, and Makomsava Females Behavioural Notes Demonstrates exceptional strategic ability: Established territory at an unusually young age through careful expansion Initially maintained small territory to avoid confrontation with larger males Systematically removed rival male genetics by eliminating cubs Shows excellent hunting abilities despite male status Maintains notably calm demeanor around vehicles Successfully defended territory against nomadic males throughout the prime Historical Significance Represents one of Londolozi’s most successful examples of male leopard strategy: Secured prime territory at just three years old Successfully expanded from initial small holding to vast territory Demonstrated perfect timing in territory acquisition and expansion Maintained genetic diversity through successful offspring The current eastern shift shows adaptation to changing dynamics and age Exemplifies successful male leopard territory acquisition and management His story particularly resonates as an example of strategic territory acquisition and management, having secured prime real estate at an unusually young age and successfully defended it through his prime years.
leopards.territory: His territory extends roughly from the Londolozi camps westwards along the Sand River over into Singita, south to most likely the Maxabene River, and slightly north of the Sand River to Sasekile Ingwe crest.

leopards.title: Hukumuri 3:3 Male
leopards.name: Hukumuri
leopards.excerpt: Large Male leopard that originated in the Kruger National Park, spent time in the north.
leopards.profile: Reports and Photographic evidence indicate that the Hukumuri Male originated in the Kruger National Park, in the Crocodile Bridge area. He initially moved north to Ngala, which is a dispersal of 130km! He then turned back south and started being seen on Londolozi in early-mid 2019. He was a contender for the northern parts of Marthly, until an altercation with either the Anderson Male, Flat Rock Male or Hosana Male left him blind in one eye in 2019. He managed to hold his own but shifted further west towards the western fenceline of the Sabi Sands Wildtuin.

leopards.title: Mawelawela 3:4 Male
leopards.name: Mawelawela
leopards.death_note: Injured by lions
leopards.excerpt: Born 2013, initially a fairly aggressive elusive male that has somewhat relaxed. Found in unconventional leopard territory of the grasslands
leopards.profile: Heritage & Lineage Born in the Sabi Sands to an unrelaxed female, his early years were marked by minimal exposure to vehicles – a factor that would significantly influence his later behaviour. His sister shared his cautious nature, highlighting the strong influence of their mother’s temperament on their development. Territory Evolution His territory establishment followed an unconventional path: Initial Phase: Arrived in Londolozi’s southwestern grasslands Establishment: Successfully took over the territory from ageing Makhotini Male Current Domain: Controls vast stretches of southwestern grasslands Recent Dynamics: Experiencing pressure from Maxims Male’s expansion and Nweti Male’s territorial shift Physical Characteristics 3:4 spot pattern Carries himself with characteristic wariness Shows battle scars from territorial conflicts Behavioural Notes The Mawelawela Male’s journey from aggressive outsider to established territorial male represents one of Londolozi’s most remarkable stories of leopard adaptation. His early encounters with vehicles were characterized by defensive displays – charging, snarling, and retreating into thick vegetation. Yet through consistent, patient viewing, a gradual transformation began to unfold. While he never developed the relaxed nature of some males, his tolerance grew enough to allow for meaningful observations of his remarkable hunting prowess. It is in his hunting behaviour that his true ingenuity shines. Where most leopards rely on ambush tactics in dense vegetation, the Mawelawela Male has mastered the art of open terrain hunting. His speciality lies in taking down prey that would intimidate many leopards – zebra foals and even giraffe calves fall prey to his strength and cunning. He moves like a ghost through the grasslands, using scattered drainage lines and ancient fig trees as staging posts for his hunts. His extensive territory, far larger than those of more conventional habitat specialists, requires careful management through regular long-distance patrols. Current Status Now in his tenth year, the Mawelawela Male faces the challenges that come with maintaining such vast territory. Recent pressure from the expanding Maxims Male and the shifting Nweti Male tests his resilience, yet he continues to adapt. His mating success with multiple females, including the Mashaba Golonyi and Jacana Females, suggests his unconventional territory choice hasn’t hindered his reproductive prospects. If anything, his mastery of the grasslands has carved out a unique niche, allowing him to thrive where other leopards might struggle. Historical Significance The Mawelawela Male’s legacy extends beyond his immediate impact on Londolozi’s leopard population. His success challenges fundamental assumptions about leopard habitat requirements and behavioural patterns. By establishing and maintaining territory in what was traditionally considered a marginal habitat, he demonstrates the remarkable adaptability of his species. His journey from aggressive outsider to successful territorial male offers hope for other challenging individuals, showing that with time and space, even the most difficult leopards can find their place in the ecosystem. Through his unique hunting specializations and territorial strategies, he has redefined what’s possible for a leopard in the open grasslands of Londolozi. His story particularly resonates as an example of successful adaptation to unconventional territory, proving that leopards can thrive in what was previously considered marginal habitat. At approximately ten years old, he now faces the typical challenge of maintaining territory against younger males, while his potential offspring in the area adds another layer of complexity to the territorial dynamics.

leopards.title: Maxim’s 5:3 Male
leopards.name: Maxim's
leopards.excerpt: Dominant since 2019. Once skittish Kruger-born giant now rules vast territory, transforming from elusive presence to formidable force.
leopards.profile: Named after ‘Maxim’s Lookout’ in Mala Mala, an area along the western bank of the Sand River. Heritage & Lineage Believed to have originated from Kruger National Park, first viewed in January 2019. His background before arriving at Londolozi remains largely unknown, though his initial skittish behaviour suggests minimal early exposure to vehicles. Territory Commands an extensive and expanding territory: Initially held eastern sections from Mala Mala to Maxabene River Expanded significantly westward by 2022-2024 Currently controls vast area from western boundary to eastern territories Primarily focused along the Sand River system Successfully pushed Senegal Bush Male westward Physical Characteristics 5:3 spot pattern The largest male currently viewed at Londolozi Impressive muscular build Distinctive golden coat Notably large tracks, easily identifiable Presumed Offspring Successfully sired multiple cubs including: Stonedrift Female (with Nkoveni Female) Xinkhova Female (with Nkoveni Female) Nsuku Male (with Three Rivers Female) Current cubs of Nkoveni Female Current cub of Three Rivers Female Current cub of Ximungwe Female Behavioural Notes Shows remarkable transformation in behaviour: Initially extremely skittish during daylight More relaxed during nocturnal hours Gradually habituating to vehicles Particularly relaxed during mating episodes Demonstrates fierce territorial defence Shows increasing confidence in vehicle presence Historical Significance Represents an important case study in: Successful leopard habituation in adulthood Territory expansion and male dominance Genetic contribution to Londolozi’s leopard population Adaptation from Kruger origins to Sabi Sands environment Currently creating a significant legacy through multiple offspring with various females A powerful reminder that even initially skittish leopards can, through patient viewing practices, become more relaxed while maintaining their wild essence.

leopards.profile: A large Male leopard is now found in the deep southwestern parts of Dudley. Initially found mostly on Sabi Sabi, but now he has pushed further north and sightings are becoming more and more regular to the west of Railway and south of Tugwaan Drive.

leopards.name: Kigelia

Cub died from a snake bite at 10 months old.

leopards.excerpt: This female leopard is found in the deep southwestern grasslands, occupying territory on what used to be her mother's territory.
leopards.profile: The daughter of the Little Bush Female, this leopard is not often seen on Londolozi soil, spending much of her time around the fringes of her mother’s territory to the south. Having said that, the southern grassland areas of Londolozi are tough places to find leopards, so it is likely that she spends more time there than we think, but sightings are infrequent. She has been viewed on a few occasions near Makhotini and Vertical Dams. Post-independence she has kept a relatively low profile but has since established territory to the south-west of Londolozi. Birthing three litters of cubs since 2019. She lost her first litter early on, the second litter was sadly killed by a snake during lockdown at 10 months old. Successfully raised both daughters in her third litter. And is now raising two more cubs born in later 2023.
leopards.territory: This female holds a territory in south west Dudley and onto our neighbours south of that. The grasslands she inhabits have less bushbuck and nyala than the areas surrounding the river but leopards here focus their attention on catching reedbuck, impala and kudu instead.

leopards.title: Nweti 4:2 Male
leopards.name: Nweti
leopards.death_note: Uncertain of cause of death
leopards.excerpt: Born 2014, dominant force in southern Londolozi. Notable for jaguar-like rosettes and exceptional hunting prowess, particularly of warthogs
leopards.profile: Named after the road in the western sector where he was first viewed Heritage & Lineage Born in December 2014 to the Hlaba’nkunzi Female and Nyelethi Male in the western sector. His exposure to vehicles from a young age contributed to his remarkably relaxed nature around game drive vehicles. Territory Evolution His territory has developed in distinct phases: Initial Phase (2017): First seen after independence from western territories Exploration Phase (2018): Expanded from Gert’s Pan to Open Areas Establishment Phase (2019): Secured territory on Sabi Sabi Current Domain: Controls vast territory including: Large sections of southern Londolozi- Southeastern Dudley Extensive areas beyond the southern boundary Territory reaching as far north as the Vlei Physical Characteristics 4:2 spot pattern Distinctive jaguar-like rosettes with spots inside Notably large and tall frame Tuft of hair on neck Impressive overall size Presumed Offspring Successfully sired multiple offspring: Nottens Male (with Ntsumi Female) Potential father to multiple cubs in his extensive territory Recently seen mating with both Mashaba and Ndzanzeni Females simultaneously Behavioural Notes Demonstrates exceptional hunting abilities: Particularly skilled at hunting warthogs Shows remarkable patience and strategy in pursuit Displays excellent problem-solving abilities Maintains calm demeanor around vehicles Shows strategic thinking in territory management Demonstrates unusual tolerance of other leopards, as seen in multiple-female mating event Historical Significance Represents an important presence in southern territories: Successfully established vast territory Shows remarkable adaptability between open grasslands and thick vegetation Provides continued leopard presence in less frequently viewed areas Passes on superior genes through successful offspring Demonstrates unusual social flexibility for a male leopard His presence in the southern territories has brought consistent leopard viewing to an area traditionally more challenging for leopard sightings, while his remarkable hunting abilities and unusual social behaviours provide new insights into leopard capabilities. Eventually moved south, establishing a territory on Sabi Sabi, but as of late 2019, he was been seen more and more in southeastern Dudley. Now becoming the dominant male in the southeastern reaches of Dudley coming as far north as the Vlei. He is a large, tall, and long male who has an incredible coat with rosettes that have spots in them that resemble those of a jaguar.

leopards.title: Hosana 3:3 Male
leopards.name: Hosana
leopards.excerpt: Born to the Karula Female, he arrived in 2018,established territory in northern Londolozi, a much loved and closely followed leopard.
leopards.profile: The name Hosana, in Xitsonga/Shangaan means “Little Chief.” Heritage & Lineage Born in February 2016 to the Karula Female in the northern sector of the Sabi Sand Reserve. While initially thought to be sired by the Tingana Male, paternity remains unconfirmed without genetic testing. Originally from the northern sector of Sabi Sand Nature Reserve, was seen a substantial amount on Djuma Territory Evolution His territory establishment followed several distinct phases: Initial Nomadic Phase (2017): First recorded on Nanga Road with a hoisted kill Exploration Phase (2018): Concentrated movements around Manyelethi River and Ximpalapala Koppie Challenge Phase (2019): Direct confrontations with Anderson Male, showing increasing confidence Dominant Phase (2019-2022): Dominant over Othawa, primarily seen along Londolozi’s western boundary Physical Characteristics 3:3 spot pattern Distinctive scar across nose from territorial disputes Yellow-green eyes Behavioural Notes Strategic approach to territory acquisition Remarkable boldness in challenging larger males, Anderson Male. Was found with three kills in the same jackalberry tree Final Status Successfully established and held territory in Othawa until his death in May 2022: Historical Significance Represents important aspects of male leopard dynamics: Played a key role in Anderson Male’s territorial decline Represented changing dynamics in the northern male hierarchy Contributed to territorial shifts north of Sand River He was very closely followed and loved by many of SafariLive’s viewers His rise to dominance in Othawa exemplified the complex dynamics of male leopard territorial establishment, particularly through his bold challenges against the previously dominant Anderson Male. His untimely death in May 2022 marked the end of a significant presence in the northwestern territories.
leopards.territory: Territorial over Othawa to the west of Marthly.

leopards.title: Misava 4:3 Male
leopards.name: Misava
leopards.excerpt: A small leopard that was forced into early independence and struggled to establish territory. Moved around eating anything it could.
leopards.profile: Being forced into early independence as his mother was killed when he was less than a year old. He then went through an incredibly challenging time fending for himself and basically had to resort to eating anything he could. As a result of the nutritional stress, his growth was stunted and at the age of six, he is still a small unthreatening leopard than sadly may never secure his own territory. He was seen catching and eating catfish from a small pool of water, monitor lizards, and tortoises in mid-2020 near the Londolozi Camps. He was not seen from then until April 2022. He has grown a little larger but is still small and unlikely to be able to challenge for territory with the current dominant males in the area as it stands.
leopards.territory: Has not yet established a territory that we are aware of.

leopards.name: Eyrefield
leopards.excerpt: Initially fairly skittish, but seems to be relaxing a bit now.
leopards.profile: Born in northern Mala Mala into a litter of three. They all made it to at least six months before the female cub was lost, all that was found was her tail in a rhino midden. Both male cubs reached independence in 2019 and the other male is now known as the Ngoboswan Male. The Eyrefield Male’s movements have been erratic recently and we are not sure where he will settle. He came to blows with the Senegal Bush Male and was then seen in the company of the Ximungwe Female in early October 2022.

leopards.excerpt: A stunning female found in the north. Successfully raised the Thumbela Female while establishing dominance in NW Marthly.
leopards.profile: Named after Xinzele road in northwestern Marthly, ‘xinzele’ meaning honeybadger in Shangaan. Heritage & Lineage Born in early 2017 to the Ingrid Dam Female and the Anderson Male. Her almost identical spot pattern to her mother’s makes her easily recognizable as part of this lineage, though she is notably smaller in size. Territory Has firmly established herself in northwestern Marthly, particularly around: Ximpalapala Koppie area Leadwood forest Manyelethi River system Rocky outcrops and boulder-strewn hillsides Areas near the northern boundary Physical Characteristics 4:4 spot pattern (nearly identical to her mother’s) Smaller frame than her mother Particularly adept at navigating rocky terrain Reproductive History Has shown increasing success in her reproductive efforts: Successful Offspring: March/April 2022: Thumbela Female (sibling lost at approximately 2 months) Previous Attempts: September 2021: First litter denned at Our Father’s Crossing (lost to nomadic male) April 2022: Two cubs (one survived – Thumbela Female) December 2024: Believed to be denning on Ximpalapala Koppie Current Status Successfully established as a territorial female in northwestern Marthly, where she has raised the Thumbela Female to independence. Known for utilizing the dramatic landscape of rocky outcrops and riverine systems for denning and hunting. Behavioural Notes Shows remarkable comfort in the challenging terrain of northwestern Marthly, particularly adept at utilizing rocky outcrops and the Manyelethi River system. Her choice of den sites demonstrates excellent maternal instincts, often selecting areas that balance accessibility with security. Despite the challenges of raising cubs near the reserve’s boundary, she has successfully adapted her movements to maintain territory while protecting her offspring. Historical Significance Represents an important presence in Londolozi’s northern territories, maintaining regular leopard viewing in an area that can be challenging to monitor. Her success in raising the Thumbela Female, particularly given the challenging landscape and proximity to the boundary, demonstrates her capabilities as a mother and territorial female. Her presence has helped maintain consistent leopard activity in the scenic but less frequently traversed northern sections of the reserve.

leopards.title: Hlambela 2:2 Male
leopards.name: Hlambela
leopards.excerpt: An impressive male, appearing as a rising force in the north. Making a name for himself by pushing other males out.
leopards.profile: Heritage & Lineage The Hlambela Male is the son of the Boulders Female and the Ravenscourt Male, both respected individuals within the greater Sabi Sands. He was given the name Hlambela , which means “he who swims” in Shangaan, inspired by his remarkable early hunting attempts that saw him wading through water in pursuit of White-faced Whistling Ducks. Territorial Movement & Dominance Initially, more skittish around vehicles, the Hlambela Male has undergone a notable behavioural shift in recent months. As he has grown in confidence, he has begun regularly patrolling a wide swath of territory that spans across the western sections of Marthly and stretches beyond Londolozi’s northern boundary. With the presumed death of the Senegal Bush Male and the eastward shift of the ageing Flat Rock Male, space has opened in the north, creating a power vacuum. The Hlambela Male has moved quickly to exploit this opportunity. Increasing pressure on the Tortoise Pan Male suggests that he may be carving out a stronghold in what was once highly contested land. His consistent scent-marking, regular presence, and bold patrols indicate that he may be establishing himself as a dominant male in the region. Physical Characteristics Broad-chested, muscular build Rich golden coat with dense rosettes Facial structure strongly reminiscent of the Ravenscourt Male Behavioural Notes The Hlambela Male is known for his extensive and purposeful movements. He is frequently encountered patrolling along the Marthly riverbeds and western boundary lines. His ability to cover long distances in short periods suggests a leopard with ambition—and the physical capability to enforce it. Early on, he displayed some nervousness around vehicles, but in recent months, he has become increasingly tolerant of vehicle presence, offering superb sightings. His comfort in diverse terrain, including riverine thickets and open grassland, speaks to his adaptability. This bodes well for his future as a territorial male, particularly in the dynamic and often unpredictable northern reaches of Londolozi. His current size and presence suggest that he is commanding attention among his rivals and establishing himself in the hierarchy of northern male leopards. With neighbouring males like the Tortoise Pan Male, Thamba Male, and possibly even the returning Ntomi Male in the broader region, the Hlambela Male’s ability to maintain and defend a core territory will be tested in the near future. Current Status Age: Born July 2018 (7 years old) Territory: Western Marthly and beyond the northern boundary; beginning to push eastward Rivals: Tortoise Pan Male, Thamba Male, possible overlap with Maxim’s Male in the river corridor Behaviour: Assertive, expanding range, increasingly relaxed around vehicles Significance and Outlook As the northern leopard dynamics continue to evolve, the Hlambela Male stands out as one of the most promising rising males. His strong lineage, physical stature, and expanding territorial presence make him a compelling figure in Londolozi’s current male hierarchy. With time, he may become the dominant male across Marthly and the surrounding regions, filling a power vacuum left by the disappearance of older leopards. His increasing tolerance for vehicle presence also means that he will likely feature more prominently in guest sightings and photographic records in the months ahead. The future of the Hlambela Male is still unfolding, but all signs suggest that he is not just passing through—he is here to stay.

leopards.title: Kangela 3:3 Male
leopards.name: Kangela
leopards.excerpt: Born 2019, nomadic explorer named for curious eyes. Early human exposure created remarkably relaxed demeanor despite nomadic challenges.
leopards.profile: Named for the Shangaan word ‘kangela’ meaning to look with curious eyes Heritage & Lineage Born in December 2019 to the Schotia Female and the Nyeleti Male on Singita property. His early exposure to humans near Singita Ebony Lodge shaped his remarkably relaxed nature. Born as part of a litter of two, though his sibling was lost at a few months of age. Territory Evolution Early Life (2019-2021): Around Singita Ebony Lodge Independence (June 2021): Began nomadic phase Exploration Phase (2023): First appeared on Londolozi’s western sections Later Phase (2023-2024): Explored northern territories, particularly Marthly Current Status: Dispersed from Sabi Sands (mid-2024) Physical Characteristics Distinctive spot pattern with black dots inside rosettes Elongated, elegant build Dark facial features around the eyes Notable battle scars along spine from territorial conflicts Not particularly large but graceful in form Behavioural Notes Demonstrated several notable characteristics: Exceptionally relaxed around vehicles Showed unusual tolerance of other young males (shared tree with Ntomi Male) Maintained a curious nature throughout the nomadic phase Historical Significance Represents interesting aspects of leopard behaviour: Demonstrates impact of early human exposure Shows unusual social tolerance for a male leopard Though his time at Londolozi was relatively brief, his story provides valuable insights into the challenges and adaptations of nomadic male leopards, particularly in their exploration of potential territories.

leopards.name: Xitsalala
leopards.death_note: Killed by the Tortoise Pan Male in a fight over a female
leopards.excerpt: Born 2019 in Ngala, ventured far south. Young nomad showing adaptability and patience while seeking territory amid northern dynamics.
leopards.profile: Named after the Shangaan word for Gardenia tree Heritage & Lineage Born in March/April 2019 to the Xitsalala Female and Tamboti Male at Ngala in the Timbavati Reserve. Born in a litter of two, with his sister also reaching independence though her current status remains unknown. Territory Evolution Early Life (2019-2021): Ngala, Timbavati Reserve Dispersal Phase: Traveled 30-40km south to Sabi Sands Current Phase: Exploring northern Londolozi, particularly around: Manyelethi River system Wild date palm thickets Potential territory amid Flat Rock Male’s eastward shift Physical Characteristics 2:2 spot pattern Sometimes appears gaunt during nomadic phase Young, developing male physique Relaxed nature around vehicles despite Timbavati origins Behavioural Notes Demonstrates notable adaptability: Shows resourceful hunting behaviour Willing to take smaller prey (recorded genet catch) Navigates complex male dynamics around Londolozi Current Status Currently exploring potential territory establishment in northern Londolozi, particularly following the presumed death of the Senegal Bush Male. Faces competition from other males including the Tortoise Pan Male and Hlambela Male for potential territory acquisition. Historical Significance Represents interesting aspects of leopard dispersal: Demonstrates long-distance male dispersal capabilities Shows adaptation to new environments Exemplifies patience in territory acquisition Currently part of significant territorial restructuring in northern Londolozi His presence in northern Londolozi adds to the complex dynamics of male leopard territory establishment, particularly during this period of significant territorial shifts.
leopards.territory: Not yet territorial on Londolozi

leopards.title: 3:2 Male
leopards.excerpt: An elusive and intriguing newcomer with an unknown past. Likely originating from the Kruger National Park, he is currently unnamed.
leopards.profile: Heritage & Origins Little is known about the 3:2 Male’s background. First seen on Mala Mala and subsequently across several reserves in the Sabi Sand system, his increasing presence in Londolozi suggests a westward dispersal typical of young males from the Kruger National Park. With no known maternal or paternal lineage in this area, he appears to be a truly wild, independent arrival, unmarked by prior habituation or familial ties to existing leopards on the reserve. His spot pattern of 3:2 gives him his temporary identifier, and distinctive physical traits include: Striking amber eyes A noticeable nick in his right ear Hairless scarring around the right eye Behavioural Notes & Habituation Initially highly skittish, the 3:2 Male has begun to show signs of becoming more relaxed around vehicles. However, he still displays typical behaviours of an unhabituated leopard: favouring dense thickets, dry riverbeds, and making himself scarce except when found on a kill. These rare sightings, often at hoisted kills, have given guides and trackers a fleeting glimpse into his secretive nature. Despite this elusive behaviour, he has begun vocalising and scent-marking in various areas of southeastern Londolozi—an early sign that he may be exploring territorial intent. This, combined with reports of him feeding near the Sand River and remaining in the same area for several days, indicates a potential interest in establishing a foothold. Current Status Age: Unknown, but likely in early adulthood (estimated 4–6 years) First sighted: 2024, on Mala Mala Recent range: Southeastern Londolozi and neighbouring reserves Habituation: Still semi-skittish but improving Behaviour: Scent-marking, patrolling, feeding on kills in prominent trees Territorial Outlook The 3:2 Male’s appearance comes at a pivotal time. With the confirmed disappearance of the Senegal Bush Male and the absence of the Nweti Male, southeastern Londolozi holds a gap in dominant male presence. Nearby females like the Xinkhova Female are reaching reproductive maturity and are likely in search of stable male territory holders. Whether the 3:2 Male will be able to establish himself remains uncertain. He may face pressure from other emerging or established males, such as the Maxim’s Male, Hlambela Male, or even the Flat Rock Male and Ntomi Male. As such, his future in this region will depend heavily on his ability to defend a territory and attract mating opportunities in the face of stiff competition. Significance & Future Potential Every new arrival reshapes the tapestry of Londolozi’s leopard population. Just as the Maxim’s Male once arrived unknown and now features prominently in the genetics of the next generation, the 3:2 Male may one day hold similar influence. His arrival marks the beginning of a story still in its early pages. With ongoing collaboration between Londolozi and neighbouring reserves, a formal name may soon be given to this mysterious male. For now, the 3:2 Male remains a figure of quiet intrigue—a powerful symbol of the ever-shifting dynamics that define life in the wild. We watch. We wait. And perhaps, we welcome.
leopards.territory: Not firmly territorial but being seen in the southeast, from the Sand River down to Shingi Dam.

leopards.title: Thumbela 4:3 Female
leopards.name: Thumbela
leopards.excerpt: Born 2022, playful daughter of Xinzele. Named for her hide-and-seek games, now confidently establishing independence in Marthly's terrain.
leopards.profile: Named after the Shangaan word for a playful hide-and-seek game played with mothers Heritage & Lineage Born in March/April 2022 to the Xinzele Female and presumably the Flat Rock Male. Born into a litter of two, though her male sibling did not survive beyond May 2022. Represents the continuation of the northern Marthly lineage. Territory Currently establishing herself in the southern portions of her mother’s territory, focusing on: Central Marthly Manyelethi Riverbed Areas around the Leadwood forest Rocky outcrops and boulder systems Physical Characteristics 4:3 spot pattern Growing confidence in her movements Particularly adept at tree climbing and boulder navigation Reproductive History Not yet of reproductive age Current Status Successfully navigating the transition to independence, showing increasing confidence in exploring her territory solo. Demonstrates excellent hunting potential during a fortuitous time of year with abundant young prey species available. Behavioural Notes Lives up to her name with a notably playful nature, particularly in her interactions with her mother during their time together. Shows remarkable comfort around vehicles despite being raised near the northern boundary where sightings were initially limited. Demonstrates growing hunting skills, particularly focused on the seasonal abundance of young prey. Her successful transition to independence has been aided by the timing, coinciding with the arrival of impala lambs, warthog piglets, and wildebeest calves. Currently developing her hunting technique, still relying more on speed and opportunistic pursuits rather than the patient stealth that will come with age. Historical Significance Represents the successful continuation of the Xinzele Female’s lineage in the northern territories. Her survival as a sole cub and successful journey to independence demonstrates the increasing stability of leopard populations in the northern sections of Londolozi. Her growing presence in central Marthly provides exciting potential for consistent viewing in this scenic part of the reserve.
leopards.territory: Fast approaching independence, being seen in southern parts of her mother's territory, Central Marthly.
